articles.title: Samsung starts rolling out stable One UI 9 with Wear OS 7 to Galaxy Watch 8 series
articles.content: TL;DR Samsung has started rolling out stable One UI 9 Watch to the Galaxy Watch 8 and Watch 8 Classic in South Korea. The Wear OS 7-based update is reaching non-beta users, ending months of testing. The update includes the October 2026 security patch, with a wider rollout expected to follow. The Galaxy Watch 9 and Watch Ultra 2 shipped with One UI 9 Watch straight out of the box. Now, Samsung is bringing its latest smartwatch software to older hardware, starting with the Galaxy Watch 8 and Watch 8 Classic . The two watches are the first to receive a stable over-the-air upgrade to the Wear OS 7-based software. Following nearly two and a half months of beta testing, Samsung has begun rolling out the stable update in South Korea. According to reports emerging on social media, the release is reaching both beta participants and regular users, marking the end of the testing period that began in August.
articles.author: Hillary Keverenge

articles.title: Surprise for Cast of 'Return of the Living Dead' Sequel. They Were Replaced by AI
articles.content: A crowdfunded sequel to the movie Return of the Living Dead was uploaded last weekend — but producer Richard Driscoll is drawing criticism for what he did to the 1985 punk/zombie classic. Kotaku reports: [The release of the movie] came to the surprise to the original cast, who were attached to star in the follow-up. Instead it seems Driscoll opted to use AI to generate the film... In 2024, Driscoll, who operates his own no-budget streaming service "DragonFLIX," launched an Indiegogo page for "TRASH's REVENGE Return of the Living Dead Universe." Unlike other fan projects, this one had a large portion of the original cast involved, with stars Randolph and Linnea Quigley acting as producers. It also threw in Quigley's fellow Sorority Babe in the Slimeball Bowl-O-Rama Michelle Bauer and the Oscar nominated Eric Roberts, who has seemingly been in everything except The Living Dead.... But after some confusion and radio silence between the cast and director, this incredible movie did not come to be. Last Halloween night, Driscoll pushed out [the almost entirely AI-generated] The Return of the Living Dead: Aftermath... The results won't surprise you. Robotic line delivery. Nonsensical sequence of events. Object impermanence. Everything's wet. Everyone looks shocked. At one point the video just flips around like you're watching on a phone someone dropped. And while the Return cast didn't film any of this footage, their likenesses are peppered throughout. "It turned out to be a fiasco," says Quigley. "I warned him, "Whatever you do, don't do any AI, because people don't like it, the fans don't like it." Living Dead alumni, even those who weren't attached to this film, have spoken out against Aftermath. They seem most concerned about the existing and continued use of their likeness, given that Driscoll has seemingly pivoted 'Trash's Revenge' into an additional project. Randolph encourages those who provided any funding to ask for a refund through their credit card company. While Romero's original film was public domain, Return of the Living Dead was not. Randolph also encourages Amazon, who bought MGM in 2022, to take legal action. A review on Reddit calls it "the worst 'film' I've ever seen," a production that "manages to not only be the worst zombie film ever made but is also the nadir of exploitation filmmaking. [T]hings quickly descend into madness and we get lots of bits of A.I. reporters out on the streets being attacked by A.I. zombies... [T]here are some A.I. cops battling it out too... Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.author: EditorDavid

articles.title: 3 best Netflix original crime dramas as rated by IMDB
articles.content: Netflix is a goldmine for crime dramas. You can find some of the most acclaimed original series the genre has ever produced there, the kind that rack up impressive IMDb scores. But which of Netflix's crop of originals are some of the best-rated and most worth your time? If you’re not sure where to start, we’ve got your back. We’ve taken care of all the digging so you can skip straight to the good stuff. The three shows below are among the best crime dramas Netflix has ever made, as rated by IMDb users. Something tells me you’ll be recommending at least one of these to someone else before long. And if you somehow haven’t gotten around to any of them yet, my advice is to fix that as soon as possible. Check them out as soon as you finish reading and get started on remedying that now. 'Narcos' One of the original Netflix powerhouses, “Narcos” kicked off the streamer’s run of must-watch crime dramas. It chronicles the bloody rise and fall of Colombian drug lord Pablo Escobar (Wagner Moura) and the DEA agents, including Javier Peña (Pedro Pascal), who spend years trying to bring him down. Blending dramatized events with real archival footage, it explores the cocaine trade’s explosive growth and the violence it unleashed across Colombia. “Narcos” is a gripping crime epic that doubles as a crash course in one of modern history’s most infamous criminal empires. So if you want something gritty and realistic, this might want to be your first stop. IMDB Rating: 8.7/10 Watch on Netflix 'Mindhunter' Executive produced by master of suspense David Fincher, "Mindhunter" is one of Netflix’s most chilling achievements. Set in the late 1970s, it follows two FBI agents, Holden Ford (Jonathan Groff) and Bill Tench (Holt McCallany) who sit down and interview imprisoned serial killers to understand how their minds work. There are no car chases or shootouts here. But there are plenty of long, unnerving conversations with some of history’s most notorious murderers. And they're starting to take a psychological toll on the men conducting them. This adventure into the minds of killers is a cerebral, slow-burn crime drama that gets under your skin, and it definitely didn't last long enough. IMDB Rating: 8.6/10 Watch on Netflix 'Ozark' Jason Bateman stars as Marty Byrde, a financial advisor who launders money for a Mexican drug cartel, until a deal goes wrong. Then, he's forced to uproot his family to the Lake of the Ozarks to make good on his debt and, most importantly, stay alive. As Marty and his wife Wendy (Laura Linney) sink deeper into the criminal underworld, they get tangled up with local crime families, the FBI, and young hustler named Ruth (Julia Garner). Bleak and gripping, this slow-burn thriller is unnervingly easy to lose a weekend to, and you probably will. IMDB Rating: 8.7/10 Watch on Netflix
articles.author: Brittany Vincent

articles.title: NVIDIA Announces New Planned Investments in Korean Startups at the MSIT-NVIDIA AI Startup Partnership Forum
articles.content: Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT and NVIDIA hosted the MSIT -NVIDIA AI Startup Partnership Forum at COEX. Ryu Je-myung, vice minister of science and ICT , joined NVIDIA leaders to meet with over 20 Korean startups across foundation models, physical AI, AI infrastructure and AI semiconductors. NVIDIA also announced an investment in Korean startup Point2 , with additional investments planned in Motif Technologies , RLWRLD and Upstage. Point2 Technology, an AI interconnect company, builds scalable, radio frequency-based interconnects that move data between chips and racks in AI factories, offering an innovative alternative to conventional copper and optical interconnect solutions for AI cluster scale-up, delivering the reach, performance and efficiency needed for next-generation AI infrastructure. Motif Technologies , a Seoul-based AI lab, develops foundation models for building AI agents that carry out complex tasks, including Motif-3, a large language model released with open weights. RLWRLD, a physical AI startup based in San Francisco, Seoul and Tokyo, develops robotics foundation models that enable humanoid and industrial robots to perform complex real-world tasks that require five-finger dexterity, such as precisely inserting components, threading nuts onto bolts and kitting parts from moving conveyors. Upstage , a Korean enterprise AI company, develops Solar language models and document AI tools that help businesses extract information from complex documents, streamline workflows and build AI applications for everyday operations. The companies represent work across the full AI stack , from infrastructure to models to robotics applications. The planned investments build on NVIDIA’s work with Korea’s startup and venture community, including more than 1,000 Korea-based members of NVIDIA Inception , a program that helps startups grow with access to preferred pricing, technical expertise and opportunities for investor introductions.
articles.author: NVIDIA Writers

articles.title: These are the 7 most vital AI terms beginners (and even power users) should know, from large language models to tokens
articles.content: In my line of work, as someone who’s constantly explaining what I do for a living, it can be a lot for someone to wrap their head around. Explaining that I cover the world of AI, the abundance of chatbots & AI agents that exist and the companies & bigwigs that throw big swaths of money at the growing tech can be a lot for someone to take in. I can only imagine how much more confused they get when they look up AI as a general search term and come across a bunch of additional technical jargon that scares them away from the trending tech altogether. I went ahead and offered up a 15-minute lesson on how to start out using ChatGPT (which helped my parents get a decent understanding of one of the most popular AI tools). Now I’m here to break down seven of the most vital terms every AI user should know. Whether you consider yourself someone who’s just starting to give AI a chance or a power user whose base level of knowledge is already strong enough, it’s still worth learning or getting a quick refresher on the world of AI. 1. Large Language Model (LLM) (Image credit: Shutterstock) A Large Language Model can be broken down easily by delving into what each letter in “LLM” stands for. The “L” represents the “large” amounts of data that it's trained on, such as the words contained in books, on sites, in articles and across research papers. The second “L” pertains to the human “language” that it’s designed to understand, process and generate on its own. And finally, the “M” represents the type of AI program that works as a “model” that interprets human patterns and relationships through words instead of just memorizing answers. For instance, an LLM taps into the patterns it’s learned during its training to properly respond to a user’s request to write a birthday message to their friend. Simply put, an LLM is the driving force behind a chatbot that helps it comprehend and generate human language. 2. Generative AI (Image credit: Shutterstock) Generative AI is a type of AI that can generate original content, such as text, images, audio, videos and computer code, based on the instruction you give it via a prompt. I’m sure you’ve come across all sorts of photos of people made to look like they exist in a neon-soaked 80s world, videos of dogs riding a skateboard like a human being and easily discernible AI-generated songs. Generative AI is used to produce those types of content as it's commanded to create something new instead of just retrieving pre-existing information. 3. Machine Learning (ML) (Image credit: Shutterstock) Think of machine learning as a method in which computers are taught how to recognize patterns and make predictions based on all the data they’ve observed. Instead of having to be given specific instructions by a programmer to complete their task, computers can rely on machine learning to learn from examples to build knowledge over time. Machine learning is comparable to the way Netflix brings up recommendations, as the streaming service analyzes what you’ve watched, what you’ve given a thumbs up to and what you've skipped to make educated decisions about what to suggest you watch next. The more information Netflix has, the stronger its recommendations will be. Machine learning is the core engine that’s crucial to the continued improvement of AI as a whole. 4. Neural Network (Image credit: Shutterstock) A neural network is a computer system that’s comparable to the human brain, as it contains layers of interconnected nodes that process information and identify patterns in the same way that neurons connect and communicate in our heads. It’s the system that helps AI recognize complicated patterns, with it being able to understand that you’re presenting it with a picture of a cat since a neural network helps it learn to recognize the patterns of that animal type. 5. Hallucinations (Image credit: Shutterstock) AI is prone to making mistakes, which are defined as hallucinations. When a chatbot confidently gives you information…

articles.title: Azahar 3DS emulator for Android gets per-game settings, major performance gains, and more
articles.content: Credit: Andy Walker / Android Authority TL;DR Azahar has just received a major update across all platforms, including Android. The 3DS emulator now offers per-game settings on Android, support for non-Snapdragon custom drivers, and a significant performance boost. The iOS version has also gained a massive performance upgrade, allowing owners of old iPhones to get in on the fun. We’ve seen several Nintendo 3DS emulators on Android in recent years, but Azahar is your best bet in 2026. The emulator has already received major updates this year, but the team says it’s now released what might be the biggest update yet. The development team has posted pre-release builds of Azahar v2127.0 on GitHub, and it says this is “arguably the single largest update we have ever published.”

articles.title: 0sec Labs Open-Sources 0, an AI Security Harness With Web UI, CLI and MCP
articles.content: Zurich-based 0sec Labs has released 0 , an open-source AI security harness. It runs vulnerability investigations, code review, pentesting, reverse engineering and fix generation. Developers drive it from a local browser console, a headless CLI or an MCP server . The 0sec Labs open-source AI security harness is licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0 and ships as a research preview. TL;DR Wrapper: It is a software harness. Bring your own LLM from 14 listed providers . Runs on: Apple Silicon macOS, x64 or ARM64 Linux, or the ghcr.io/0sec-labs/0 container. No GPU needed. Model inference runs at your provider. Performance: Strong self-reported CTF scores, plus a public record of upstream Linux kernel fixes. Best: 93/95 (97.9%) on XBOW web CTFs, gpt-5.4 cohort, any-success grouping. Worst: Black-box-only XBOW union of 81/104 (77.9%) . A 2026 cold run scored 45/104 (43.3%) . Bottom line: Best: one harness spans web, source, packages, binaries and kernels. Worst: headline scores are self-reported and not pass@1. What is 0 from 0sec Labs? 0 is a control plane around LLMs and security tools. It is not a model. You plug in a provider, and 0 runs scoped workflows against authorized targets. The research team describes it as a self-evolving, multi-model harness . 0sec Labs is backed by Y Combinator . How does the 0 harness work? The architecture docs state one rule: reproduce before trusting. Agentic scans follow a conceptual pipeline: Plan, Discover, Attack: a research agent picks vulnerability classes, maps endpoints and tests hypotheses. Triage: filters remove weak findings and check evidence completeness. Verify: a separate session re-exercises each candidate, with 5 turns per finding. Report: outputs include HTML, PDF, SARIF, Markdown and JSON. Web pentesting is shell-first. The agent uses bash with curl, python3 and sqlmap, not a fixed HTTP tool set. Evidence carries a proof grade from candidate to impact-proven . Compiled targets go through 0verse , a separate in-repo engine. It wraps Ghidra, angr and AFL++. Its local MCP server exposes 9 tools for scanning, triage, PoVs and reports. How do developers use it? Installation is one script. Running 0 opens the local browser console without an account. The console has chat, a findings queue and board, workflow templates, skills and memory. Coding agents connect through 0 mcp-server --workflows . The CLI exposes the same workflow runner with commands like 0 workflow run and 0 runs list . Model access is bring-your-own. The API keys page lists OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, OpenRouter, Azure, Qwen, Kimi, GLM and Grok. It also supports Claude, Codex and Gemini CLI runtimes. Benchmarks: what do the numbers say? All scores below are self-reported. Benchmark Score Conditions XBOW web CTFs 93/95 (97.9%) gpt-5.4 cohort, any retained success counts XBOW union, white-box 102/104 Retained artifacts, not additive XBOW union, black-box 81/104 Retained artifacts, not additive Cybench 36/40 (90.0%) Azure gpt-5.4, 3 retries npm audit, 81 packages F1 0.973 100% TPR, FPR 0.11, self-built ground truth The recorded cost was about $5.20 per solved XBOW challenge . How does 0 compare with other open-source AI pentesting tools? Feature 0 (0sec Labs) Shannon (Keygraph) Strix CAI (Alias Robotics) License MIT OR Apache-2.0 AGPL-3.0 Apache-2.0 MIT + proprietary research-only Status Research preview Active Active Archived Aug 28, 2026 Interfaces Web console, CLI, MCP server CLI, CI actions CLI, local web viewer, agent skills CLI/REPL, MCP support Scope Web, LLM, MCP, source, packages, binaries, kernel Web apps and APIs, source required Code, web apps, APIs General offensive and defensive automation Binary reverse engineering Yes, 0verse (Ghidra) Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Models BYO, 14 listed providers BYO, Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, Bedrock, local BYO via LiteLLM 300+ via LiteLLM Requirements macOS (Apple Silicon) or Linux Docker, Node.js 18+ Docker Python 3.12 recommended What has 0 found in the wild? articles.title: Samsung could soon start charging for Galaxy AI with a new $4.99 Premium subscription
articles.content: TL;DR Samsung could reportedly start offering a paid Galaxy AI Premium subscription. It could offer new Galaxy AI features and four times higher usage limits than the free tier. It could cost $4.99 per month or $47.99 annually. Samsung started offering Galaxy AI on its smartphones a few years ago, and it has always been available for free on compatible Samsung phones. However, if you are one of the few people who use Galaxy AI extensively, you may want to prepare to shell out a few bucks for it soon. According to a new report from SammyGuru , Samsung could be prepping to offer a new Galaxy AI Premium subscription. It appears to be part of an early access program, allowing users to opt in and test it. Screenshots shared by the outlet say that any funds users spend during the test period will be refunded once testing concludes. That is an effective way to get more users to try the various tiers and provide Samsung with useful data.

articles.title: DroidDeck PC game emulator for Android now supports your Pixel and Exynos-powered Galaxy phones too
articles.content: Credit: Hadlee Simons / Android Authority TL;DR DroidDeck, a PC games emulator for Android, now supports a wider range of devices. After originally being restricted to flagship Snapdragon chips, DroidDeck now also supports MediaTek, Google Tensor, and Samsung Exynos chips. The team also added a dual-screen interface where one screen runs a regular Linux desktop or shows performance stats. The growing power of mobile devices and the ease of running or emulating x86 software directly on Arm64 hardware have made PC emulation popular in recent years. Among the chief PC emulation tools for Android, DroidDeck has quickly become one of our favorites because it lets you play titles from your Steam library and recently added support for both Xbox Cloud Gaming as well as running Game Pass titles locally. And with all of that, it adopts a Steam OS-style interface. However, the app only worked on high-end Snapdragon chips until now, but that’s changing as it adds support for more APUs. The team behind DroidDeck has rolled out another major update with version 0.70, introducing support for non-Qualcomm GPUs. According to the release notes on GitHub , the PC emulation tool now supports Mali, PowerVR, and Xclipse GPUs, essentially enabling support for MediaTek Dimensity and Helio series, Google Tensor, and Samsung Exynos lineups. When you launch DroidDeck on Android hardware, it will automatically search for the relevant drivers based on the chipset.

articles.title: Dev error bricked 600 PCs, caused $1M CD-ROM write-off
articles.content: Welcome to Monday, the day upon which The Register offers a new instalment of " Who, Me? " – our reader-contributed column that shares your stories of messing up, 'fessing up, and somehow finding redress. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Oriel" who told us he once worked for a vendor of small business accounting software. This story comes from a time when software shipped on CD-ROMs and users bought it off the shelf in actual shops. The vendor released a new version each year and always shipped it before a major holiday that's celebrated with a giant meal. Oriel was part of the team whose job it was to get the package ready on time. In the previous year, they flubbed the job because the program didn't always install itself on some PCs running Windows 95 or Windows ME machines system due to registry corruption. "We wanted to increase our successful installation metrics, so in conjunction with the installation team, a key decision was made – by me – to force the updating of registry keys to enable the install," Oriel admitted. In his email to The Register , he asked the portentous question: "What could possibly go wrong?" What went wrong was that not long after the software was shipped, the vendor's support lines started getting calls from customers who complained that after installing the accounting package none of their other software would work. "Installing a new version of our application had borked the customer's machine completely," Oriel wrote. The company decided the best thing to do was to tell affected customers they should go and buy a new PC – and that it would pick up the bill, no questions asked. "In the week prior to the holiday, we replaced over 600 machines," Oriel told The Register . Oriel and his developer colleagues were of course told to fix the problem but couldn't reproduce it nor figure out their mistake. "To get a reproduction case we need a user's machine where the user had created a Windows Registry restore point prior to installing our application," Oriel explained. If the developers could find such a machine, the plan was to roll it back to the restore point, verify everything was in order before the customer installed the update, install the accounting software, and figure out the problem. The company tasked its support agents with finding a customer willing to surrender their PC, which proved difficult because few bothered to create a registry restore point. The day before the holiday, a customer volunteered their machine. This customer was located a few hours away by road, so an engineer got the job of visiting on the morning of the holiday to pick up the stricken machine, give the customer a shiny new system and configure it to their specifications. Said engineer did the job, which took so long he was invited to stay for the holiday meal, then returned to HQ with the broken box. The next day, Oriel and his colleagues got to work and found a fix, then created a version of the accounting application that wouldn't break any more PCs. Oriel was, of course, summoned into a meeting with senior execs to explain the situation and watched as they decided the best course of action was to pull buggy CDs from stores – which meant trashing CDs and packaging valued at $1 million. Have you made a mistake that broke customers' kit, or cost millions? If so, don't make the mistake of not sharing your story with The Register and click here to email the column. ®

articles.title: Apple’s $2,899 MacBook PROLED hides a massive unified memory bottleneck — why I think power users should abandon macOS for Nvidia RTX Spark and AMD Strix Halo
articles.content: If you read any review for Apple’s new MacBook Pro , you will see a lot of folks drooling over the new PROLED XDR display. And they’re not wrong — flawless color calibration, a new touchscreen interface and up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness. But if you look past the shiny new Dynamic Island, you’ll see a darker reality. One where what I like to call “OLED washing” is happening. Apple didn’t build a machine for the next generation of computing (local AI). They built a $2,899 luxury item. If you want to see what a real, weaponized local AI computer looks like in 2026, you need to look away from Cupertino and start looking more closely at the better value-for-money monsters being built with Nvidia’s RTX Spark and AMD’s Strix Halo inside. The elephant in the room: memory (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Yes, we are currently living through RAMageddon , a brutal memory shortage driven by enterprise data centers hoarding silicon. While I do see cracks in this cloud AI bubble, it’s going to be here for a while. Apple’s response to this was to slap a near-three racks starting price on the 14-inch PROLED MacBook Pro and give you a paltry 24GB of unified memory. It’s both overkill in some ways — that tandem OLED screen might be worth it if you are a Hollywood color grader editing 8K ProRes video for example. But in others, for those moving into the era of ditching the data center and running local agentic AI directly on our hardware — 24GB is a tough pill to swallow. It’s effectively a multi-million dollar mansion with only one bathroom. It looks gorgeous from the street, but the moment you invite guests over (or spin up a local 70B parameter LLM), the plumbing completely collapses. The portable data centers taking its place (Image credit: Future) While Apple is obsessing over making their chassis lighter and adding a touchscreen nobody asked for, the Windows ecosystem has been quietly preparing for a value war. Just a few weeks ago, I balked at the high $5,899 price tag for the 128GB version of the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra that I tested. And then, I saw the equivalently-specced 14-inch MacBook PROLED come in at $7,099 ($7,399 for the 16-inch). (Image credit: Future) And yes, the PROLED does have a much better display, better CPU performance and a longer battery life. But, are those uplifts worth an additional $1,200? I’m not sure. Benchmark RTX Spark (Surface Laptop Ultra) M5 Pro (MacBook Pro) Waterloo Battle Analysis prompt (Meta Llama 3.1 8B) 61.26 tok/sec 0.51s time to first token 52.69 tok/sec 0.69s time to first token Apollo space program history prompt 67.51 tok/sec 0.09s time to first token 53.66 tok/sec 0.13s time to first token Plus if you are leaning more towards local AI, the tokenomics of an RTX Spark are a little better than M5 Pro too. M5 Max is faster, but you'll have to pay much more for that (as you can see). If the tandem OLED is important, then the MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI+ may have a terrible name, but at $6,799, it’s still $300 less. More bang for your buck with team red (Image credit: Future) And I haven’t even gotten to the AMD side of things yet. The Strix Halo chip has grown into quite the AI-capable silicon over its life. And that longevity means you can find some good options with more money for much less money than taking a bite of the Apple. TUF Gaming A14 (AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 392, 32GB RAM): was $2199 now $2149 This is definitely one for those with more of a gaming persuasion, but it's a strong chip for local AI workloads with 8GB more memory than the MacBook Pro for much less. View Deal Yoga Pro 7a (AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 388, 32GB RAM): $2299 If you don't want to give up the slick utilitarian aesthetic and the OLED display, the Yoga Pro 7a is the option to go for. Still more memory, and still $600 less. View Deal ROG Flow Z13 (AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, 128GB RAM): $3299 Taking things to the next level is what's essentially a far superior Surface Pro with a monster amount of memory. articles.title: Android Auto drops Android 9 and 10 as Google confirms new minimum requirements
articles.content: TL;DR Google has officially raised Android Auto’s minimum requirement for wired connections from Android 9 to Android 11. The change confirms our October report about Android 10 users receiving warnings that support was ending. Phones stuck on Android 9 or 10 are no longer officially supported, with affected users already reporting that Android Auto has stopped working. Every few years, Google raises the bar for the oldest Android versions that can still run Android Auto . Android 6 lost its place in 2022, followed by Android 8 in 2024 . Now, two more versions are reaching the end of the road, and Google has officially confirmed Android 11 as the new minimum requirement for wired Android Auto connections. The change now appears on Google’s updated Android Auto support page , which previously listed Android 9 Pie as the minimum requirement for connecting a phone to a compatible car via USB. With Android 11 now taking its place, both Android 9 and Android 10 have fallen outside the officially supported range.

articles.title: I tried this viral budget hack for winter greenhouses—here’s how
articles.content: With cold temperatures and frosty soil, winter is hard enough for your existing garden let alone trying to plant any new seeds. And, if like me, you're lacking indoor space and don't have an external greenhouse then this hack might be the game changer you're looking for. I've been researching about setting up my own mini greenhouses while I wait to plant these 7 winter-hardy vegetables in February . While there were several ideas on what to buy, I stumbled across a TikTok that said I could make them pretty easily yourself – and all I'd need is a milk jug. So, I thought I'd give it a try. Here's what happened. How does it work? @sandra.maria.home ♬ original sound - Sandra Sharing DIY home and garden tips on TikTok, @sandra.maria.home has almost 65k followers watching her videos, but it was what she had to say about milk jugs that really caught my attention. In one video, she explains: "This is a milk jug greenhouse method I have perfected over the years. A mini greenhouse lets you start seeds outdoors way earlier without grow lights or without bathing seedlings inside. For me, it's the start of the growing season." And all you need is a milk jug (or several, depending on how many seed starters you're planning), a pair of scissors, a kitchen knife and some duct tape. And, of course, some soil and your seeds. Then, follow these five simple steps: Wash your jugs out to avoid any mold and throw away the lids Cut the jug in half using a knife or scissors Use the knife/scissors to make some drainage holes in the bottom Fill the bottom half with appropriate soil and plant your seeds Seal with duct tape Sandra has some advise from her years of mini greenhouse making when it comes to the soil you choose: "Don't use anything with fertilizer, it's too harsh for the seedlings and will kill them." And, if you're planning on planting multiple seeds, use a pen or wax pencil to number the jugs so you don't lose track of which ones are which. Once spring comes around, you can gently release the duct tape and let the plants acclimatize for planting in your yard. If you haven't already got duct tape lying around the house, you can pick it up for just under $4 to secure the edges of your mini greenhouse. It's durable, heavy duty and has excellent adhesion. If your duct tape is struggling to stick in the cold, Sandra recommends heating it up with a hair dryer. View Deal Here's what happened when I tried it (Image credit: Future) While Sandra says she picks her jugs up at her local coffee shop, which is a seriously clever idea, I live in a busy household where we happen to drink a lot of milk. Or, at least enough for me to collect a few jugs myself. So, milk jugs in hand, I followed her steps using scissors to cut and make drainage holes as I found this a lot easier. I then lined them up in my yard in a place I knew I could keep an eye on them without having to venture too far. (Image credit: Future) Another piece of advice that I think is worth mentioning from Sandra's video is that she says to densely pack the seeds in since this small jug of soil won't be their forever home. That means there will be more to move over once spring rolls around and they can grow into their new environment. Sure, I need to wait and see how effective my mini greenhouses actually are when spring comes around, but I'm happy that I didn't waste any money and hardly any time doing it. So, if some seeds are successful and others aren't, I'll still be happy to try again. What I loved about this gardening hack is that making the mini greenhouses really took me no time at all – and it also didn't cost me anything. Considering how easy and affordable this hack is, I'll definitely be recommending it to friends. I just might wait until next year, so I can show them proof that it really does work. articles.title: 1 in 4 data centers sits in a water-stressed area — here’s what that means for nearby communities
articles.content: AI has become integrated into our lives whether we like it or not. Despite big tech forcing schools to choose and lawsuits highlighting its dangers, the controversial technology is here to stay. New research published in Environmental Science & Technology puts specific AI concerns on a global map, highlighting 9,347 identified data centers, with roughly a quarter located in areas where water demand would exceed available supply for at least one month a year. The water has to come from somewhere (Image credit: Dan Bracaglia/Tom's Guide) Data centers use water to remove heat from their equipment. In evaporative cooling systems, some of that water evaporates rather than returning to the local water system. Electricity generation and hardware manufacturing add an indirect water footprint, too, according to the Pacific Institute . Where and when that consumption happens matters. The institute warns that data center water demand peaks during hot, dry periods, when supplies may be constrained, and other users also need more. Meeting those peaks can require additional utility infrastructure and spending. “They are landing on top of the water supply of cities and farms,” study lead author Lorenzo Rosa said in an American Chemical Society release . That makes data center construction relevant to people who may never pay for an AI subscription . Before approving a facility, a community needs to understand whether its water system can accommodate a large new customer during a dry summer. Cities and municipalities are the largest water users, accounting for nearly 41% of the facilities studied, while agriculture is the primary user, accounting for another 28%, according to the American Chemical Society. A yearly average can miss the pressure (Image credit: Future) The Potomac River basin offers a useful example. An analysis by the Interstate Commission on the Potomac River Basin describes current average data center water consumption in the Washington metropolitan area as relatively small. Its estimated 2025 average was about 4 million gallons a day, with peak-day consumption of approximately 15 million gallons. Cooling choices help explain the variation. Around 40% of facilities in the analysis rely exclusively on air cooling, while many others take advantage of cooler winter weather to reduce cooling demands. The commission cautions that approaches using less water often require more energy. For residents, an annual consumption figure only answers part of the question. They also need to know how much water a facility could require during the hottest days, when local supplies may already be under pressure. What communities deserve to know (Image credit: Shutterstock) The same global study also examined existing data center locations under a scenario of 3°C of global warming relative to around 1900. The share exposed to water shortages rose to roughly a third. That projection applies future climate conditions to the facilities identified in the study; it doesn’t account for where additional data centers might be built. Better disclosure would make proposed projects easier to assess. The Pacific Institute identifies a lack of standardized reporting on data center size, location and water use as an obstacle for communities and water managers. Residents deserve clear answers about a proposed facility’s water source , expected summer demand and plans for drought. They also deserve to know who would pay for any necessary infrastructure upgrades. What communities can do now (Image credit: Getty Images/erika-giraud) If a data center is proposed near your home, get answers now. Start with your local planning board or water utility and ask where its cooling water would come from, how much it could use on the hottest days, and what would happen during a drought. Be direct and ask who would pay for any water-system upgrades, too, and whether the operator would be required to make its water use public. Those details can help residents assess a…

articles.title: 6 biggest new shows to stream this week —including 'Lord of the Rings' and Anthony Mackie's bank heist thriller
articles.content: It’s dark by 5 p.m., the holiday ads have started and I’ve stopped pretending I want to do anything else but rot on the couch. Perfect timing, because TV is stacked. As a streaming editor who watches TV for a living, I’ve rounded up the biggest new and returning shows to watch this week across Netflix, Prime Video, Apple TV and more of the best streaming services . This week, we're heading back to Middle-earth for more epic fantasy in "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" season 3, while a new heist thriller, "12 12 12," promises twists and turns. "The Good Daughter" digs into family secrets and dark drama, and the ladies of "The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County" are ready to serve up a helping of reality TV mess. The days are getting shorter, but your watchlist is getting longer. Here’s what to watch this week. ‘The Body’ (Netflix) The vibes: “Yellowjackets” meets “Carrie” at a sleepover. The plot: When a dance-team initiation goes very wrong, a clique of Catholic schoolgirls finds itself dealing with more than just the usual teenage drama. After a drug-fueled ritual leaves new recruit Grace (Sofia Wylie) acting strangely, her fellow Lions begin experiencing prophetic visions. Soon, the whole town is gripped by supernatural panic. Premiere date: All 8 episodes on Wednesday, Nov. 11 at 3 a.m. ET Where to watch: Netflix ‘The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power’ season 3 (Prime Video) The vibes: Middle-earth is having a collective meltdown. The plot: Five years after Sauron (Charlie Vickers) decimated the Elves, the Dark Lord is closer than ever to conquering Middle-earth. There's just one little snag: He still hasn't perfected the One Ring. As he works out the kinks, Galadriel (Morfydd Clark), Elrond (Robert Aramayo) and the other free peoples must put aside their differences and stop him. Oh, and Galadriel's husband, Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) is back. Premiere date: Episodes 1-4 on Wednesday, Nov. 11 at 3 a.m. ET Where to watch: Prime Video ‘The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County’ (Hulu) The vibes: California, here come the Mormon wives! The plot: MomTok is going West(er), and they’re bringing plenty of baggage. A new crop of influencer moms is navigating the fault lines between traditional LDS values and California's more relaxed take on faith. With Utah transplant Jen Affleck in the mix alongside non-Mormon stars Bobbi Althoff and Aspyn Ovard, expect clashing worldviews, messy marriages and friendships with very little staying power. Premiere date: All 10 episodes on Thursday, Nov. 12 at 12 a.m. ET Where to watch: Hulu ‘The Good Daughter’ (Peacock) The vibes: Southern Gothic sister therapy, with a body count. The plot: Two decades after violence tore their family apart, sisters Charlotte (Meghann Fahy) and Samantha Quinn (Rose Byrne) are still living with the fallout. When a similar attack rocks their Georgia hometown, Charlotte finds herself at the center of a new investigation. Solving it means reopening old wounds and reckoning with a family history packed with secrets. Premiere date: All 6 episodes on Thursday, Nov. 12 at 3 a.m. ET Where to watch: Peacock ‘The Empress’ season 3 (Netflix) The vibes: One last, bodice-ripping trip to the imperial court The plot: In the final season of the hit German drama, Elisabeth (Devrim Lingnau) fights for her marriage and her place in the empire, while a devastating war leaves Franz (Philip Froissant) traumatized and unfaithful. A trip abroad sparks an unexpected connection with Hungarian revolutionary Count Andrássy (Dejan Bućin), as Maximilian (Johannes Nussbaum) heads to Mexico to claim a crown of his own. Premiere date: All 6 episodes on Thursday, Nov. 12 at 3 a.m. ET Where to watch: Netflix ‘12 12 12’ (Apple TV) The vibes: A little “The Italian Job,” a little “Heat,” a little “The Fugitive.” The plot: Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan face off in this eight-part thriller about a massive bank robbery in Zurich. articles.title: I ditched my other tracking cards for this one that looks incognito in my wallet — here’s why
articles.content: ​Over the past year, I’ve tested dozens of Bluetooth trackers, from household names like the AirTag 2 to specialized safety devices like the Pebblebee Halo . While wallet-sized tracking cards are convenient, most suffer from the same fatal flaw: they look like trackers that easily distinguish themselves over other cards you might carry. ​Anyone digging through a stolen wallet can spot an odd plastic slab immediately and toss it. However, the Statik SmartCard Incognito solves this by hiding in plain sight with a realistic credit card design. And now, it's found a permanent spot whenever I switch to a standard MagSafe wallet without support for Apple's Find My service. With a design that lets it hide in plain sight, disguised as an ordinary credit card, the Statik SmartCard Incognito could dupe thieves to believe it's like any other card in your wallet. Powered by an rechargeable battery rated for 11 months with universal Qi wireless charging and seamless support for both Apple Find My and Google Find Hub, it's a Bluetooth tracking card that delivers total peace of mind. View Deal Blending in with the rest (Image credit: John Velasco / Tom's Guide) ​Most tracking cards are dead giveaways in a wallet. Between their extra bulk and distinct matte or glossy finishes, they rarely look like payment cards. Models I’ve tested previously, like the original Nomad Tracking Card and the Rolling Square AirCard Pro , practically scream "Bluetooth tracker." ​The closest any device came to flying under the radar was the Nomad Tracking Card Pro, which swapped the transparent circuit-board aesthetic for clean, uniform aluminum. But the Statik SmartCard Incognito takes disguise a step further by ditching the gadget look entirely in favor of an authentic credit card disguise. (Image credit: John Velasco / Tom's Guide) ​With a faux magnetic stripe on the back, a simulated chip on the front, and realistic details down to an expiration date, it blends effortlessly into a stack of plastic. Better yet, at just 1.8 mm thick, it easily undercuts the Nomad Tracking Card Pro’s bulkier 2.5 mm frame. All the tracking features I need (Image credit: John Velasco / Tom's Guide) ​While I appreciate the clever design, what matters most is actually being able to track it down. Luckily, the Statik SmartCard Incognito checks off all the boxes and delivers everything I could ask for in an everyday wallet tracker. ​One of its best perks is dual compatibility: it supports both Apple Find My and Google’s Find Hub network, whereas many competing trackers require buying separate models for each ecosystem. That means I can pair it with either an iPhone or an Android device, making it an effortless stocking stuffer for just about anyone since it’s platform-agnostic. ​Just like standard tracking cards, I can pinpoint its location through the Find My app on my iPhone — complete with a map overview, battery status, and the option to display contact details if it's placed in Lost Mode. I can also share the tracker with family members, which is especially handy for shared items like travel pouches or key wallets. ​If I misplace my wallet nearby, I can ping the SmartCard Incognito to play a loud chime through its built-in speaker. I can’t tell you how many times that simple alert has saved me when rushing out the door for my morning commute. Wireless charging convenience (Image credit: John Velasco / Tom's Guide) ​While plenty of ultra-slim trackers still force you to keep track of finicky proprietary dongles, the Statik SmartCard Incognito embraces universal wireless charging. ​Statik managed to squeeze a 150 mAh rechargeable cell into its razor-thin frame, delivering up to 11 months of tracking per charge. Instead of hunting down replacement coin-cell batteries like you have to with an AirTag, you just drop this onto any Qi charging pad or flat MagSafe stand for a quick recharge. There are no bespoke cables to lose, making the maintenance virtually frictionless. ​At $29, the…

articles.title: T-Mobile’s T-Mix perk changes come with a 90-day lock-in and a $15 catch
articles.content: TL;DR T-Mobile T-Mix customers can change their subscription Picks during the final 10 days of each 90-day cycle. Missing the window means existing subscription perks automatically carry over into the next cycle. A $15 charge per eligible partner perk allows customers to release it early for a phone promotion, while T-Mobile’s own perks remain changeable anytime. T-Mobile’s new T-Mix plans promise something wireless customers have wanted for years: more control over what they’re paying for. But that freedom comes with a few ground rules, including a limited window to change perks and a potential $15 charge if you need to switch early. Unveiled last month, T-Mix lets customers choose benefits such as Netflix, Xbox Game Pass, and phone deals instead of getting the same set of extras as everyone else. These benefits are called Picks, and customers can change their selections every 90 days. However, that flexibility goes beyond what T-Mobile’s initial announcement explained.

articles.title: I swam 1400m with the Apple Watch 12 and Fitbit Edge: Here’s which fitness tracker came out on top
articles.content: Both the Apple Watch Series 12 and the Fitbit Edge are designed to do more than just count your steps, calories and sleep. They can both track multiple sports, but which one comes out on top in the water? I swam 1400 metres with both devices, using my Speedo smart goggles as the control — read on to find out more. Before we dive into the data, check out our Apple Watch Series 12 review and Fitbit Edge review on Tom’s Guide here. I swam 1400m with the Apple Watch 12 and Fitbit Edge: Here’s which fitness tracker came out on top Let’s start with how these trackers measure your swimming workouts. Both use an internal accelerometer and gyroscope to recognise arm pulls and calculate how many strokes you take per length, as well as your stroke rate (strokes per minute). That said, there is a slight difference between the two trackers. Before starting a swim workout, the Apple Watch Series 12 asks you to confirm the length of the pool you’re swimming in. This means during the workout, you’re able to see at a glance how many lengths you’ve swum. The Fitbit Edge doesn’t have a similar feature. When you get out of the pool, the Apple Watch will also give you a breakdown of how far you swam in each stroke, whereas the Fitbit Edge doesn’t. As a control, I used my Speedo iQ Vanisher 3.0 goggles. These smart goggles give you a wealth of data when you’re back on dry land. As well as your pace, distance, and how long you spent resting at the side of the pool, you’ll also be able to see your head position, breath time and distance per stroke for each stroke. Here’s what the Apple Watch Series 12 and Fitbit Edge recorded: Speedo iQ Vanisher 3.0 Apple Watch Series 12 Fitbit Edge Distance 1440m 1440m 1760m Pace 2:25 mins/100m 2:27 mins/100m 2:01 mins/100m Lengths 72 72 77 Strokes Breaststroke: 840m, Freestyle: 600m Breaststroke: 840m, Freestyle: 600m N/a Heart rate N/a 129 bpm 126 bpm As you can see from the data, the Apple Watch Series 12 was pretty perfect in the pool, measuring exactly what my goggles did. While the goggles don’t record heart rate, according to my Oura Ring 5 , my average over the course of the swim was 129 beats per minute. The Fitbit Edge, on the other hand, recorded a longer swim, and therefore a few more lengths. It would be nice to see stroke data on the fitness tracker, but again, I’d argue that the Edge is designed for the casual swimmer, not someone looking for a wealth of data. Either way, I was impressed with the accuracy of the Apple Watch in the water. Being able to input the length of the pool and see at a glance how many lengths I’d covered allowed me to listen to my podcast (the Shokz OpenSwim Pro headphones are still my go-to) without having to keep count. During most swim workouts, I typically switch strokes every 10 lengths, so it’s a good addition to have. I’ll be continuing to test wearables in the pool, but which of these devices would you be more interested in? Let us know in the poll below. articles.title: Asahi Linux Drops MIT and Goes Full GPL After Spotting LLM-Assisted License Laundering
articles.content: It's FOSS reports: Asahi Linux is the reason you can run Linux on an Apple Silicon Mac today. For years, the project put most of its own code under the MIT license so that anyone, including the BSDs, could reuse it as needed... They have announced that Asahi is moving all of its repositories to the GNU General Public License version 2 or later. Going forward, all Asahi Linux code will be under strong copyleft licenses only. Asahi Linux compares their dilemma to the 1990s, when "permissively licenced projects were viewed by tech companies as free real estate to pilfer and exploit," adding that "Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it... The malicious practices of the 90s and 2000s have reared their ugly heads once again, this time driven in large part by both the insatiable appetite of frontier AI labs for high-quality training data, and militant animosity toward the Free Software community." In short, they argue that for Asahi Linux, using the permissive MIT license "is no longer viable." Some time ago, we were made aware of multiple attempts to exploit our permissive licensing to hijack our work, with a direct view to replacing the project and aggressively monetising Linux on Apple Silicon. In some extreme cases, in-development feature code was being lifted straight out of our personal forks and published without attribution or lazily rewritten with LLM assistance to obfuscate its origin. The MIT licence explicitly allows this, and has no carveouts to protect against bad faith actors. As such, we made the difficult decision to begin the process of transitioning all of our repositories to the GNU General Public License version 2 or later. Going forward all Asahi Linux code will be licenced under strong copyleft licences only. It's FOSS explains that "Under the GPL, anyone who distributes a modified version has to release the source under the same license. You can't legally build a closed, paid Apple Silicon distro on top of GPL code. And if a product's source has to be public, the copying is easier to spot." And their article also points out that before AI, bad actors attempting code laundering "usually meant manually rewriting code line by line, renaming variables and stuff, and shuffling functions around until it no longer looked like the original. LLMs made it much more easy and cheaper of course." In case you did not know, Asahi Linux forbids AI generated code contribution... As far as I can tell, this is the first time a major open source project has moved to copyleft specifically because of AI-assisted code laundering. Projects have relicensed before, but usually to stop cloud providers from reselling their work as a service. This one is specifically about AI... The move has drawn criticism, particularly from the BSD side, which was one of the main reasons Asahi chose MIT in the first place. OpenBSD's Apple Silicon support relies on Asahi's m1n1 bootloader. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: 3 calendar and text scams circulating right now, and how to avoid them
articles.content: We’ve all gotten the text message claiming a package couldn’t be delivered because of an incomplete address. But scammers are getting a lot more creative, and they’re weaponizing the built-in notification systems on your phone to get your attention. Instead of just sending emails that end up in your spam folder, they’re injecting fake events directly into your calendar and spoofing group text messages to bypass your carrier’s basic filters. Here’s how to spot the newest wave of mobile scams and quarantine them without compromising your device. Nuke rogue calendar subscriptions If your calendar is suddenly flooded with alerts claiming your phone has a virus or you’ve won a prize, you haven’t actually been hacked. You accidentally clicked a malicious pop-up on a website that subscribed you to a spam calendar. To fix it on an iPhone, go to Settings, tap Calendar, and tap Accounts. Look for Subscribed Calendars, find the one you don’t recognize, and tap Delete Account. The spam will vanish instantly. On Google Calendar, go to calendar.google.com on a computer (it’s much easier to manage subscriptions on a computer than the mobile app). Look at the left sidebar under Other calendars. Hover over the spam calendar you don’t recognize and click the X icon to remove the calendar. Ignore the address update text The package delivery scam is incredibly effective right now. You’ll get a text claiming a delivery is suspended, complete with a link to a fake postal service website asking for a small redelivery fee. The postal service doesn’t send texts from random 10-digit numbers. Never click the link. Instead, copy the tracking number if there is one and paste it directly into the official shipping website yourself to see if it’s legit or not. Silence the chaotic group text spam Scammers are now dumping 20 or so random phone numbers into a single group text containing a malicious link. Once one person replies to ask who everyone is, your phone starts buzzing nonstop. Don’t reply. Open the message thread, tap the group icon at the top, scroll down, and tap Leave this Conversation or Leave Group. Reporting the group as spam produces a similar result.

articles.title: Korea Advances Physical AI Across Industries With NVIDIA
articles.content: Tapping into the country’s strengths in manufacturing and engineering, NVIDIA is helping advance Korea’s physical AI ecosystem. The country’s industry leaders are applying accelerated computing, AI and simulation to everything from semiconductor manufacturing to robotics and autonomous vehicles. These efforts are helping bring physical AI from development into real-world production. Samsung Advances Semiconductor Engineering With Accelerated Computing and AI Physics Samsung Electronics is expanding its collaboration with NVIDIA to advance semiconductor innovation through accelerated computing and AI physics. The work spans materials research, process development and device engineering. In technology computer-aided design, Samsung is working with NVIDIA cuISS and NVIDIA cuDSS to accelerate computations involving sparse linear systems. The collaboration also extends to GPU acceleration for process and optical simulations. In materials research, Samsung’s sMOL platform has run selected quantum chemical calculations up to 5x faster end to end with NVIDIA cuEST . Samsung is also exploring NVIDIA cuEquivariance to speed up tensor operations used in training and inference for atomistic AI models. Samsung is developing chip-scale thermal and mechanical analysis workflows with NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo . In one AI homogenization case, combining AI-predicted effective material properties, coarser grids and GPU acceleration resulted in a roughly 1,600x speedup. Simulation time fell from about 18 hours for a fine-grid solve on a 32-core CPU to 41 seconds for a GPU-accelerated coarse-grid solve. Looking ahead, NVIDIA Agent Toolkit could connect these simulation tools and AI models, helping future engineering agents run analyses and compare design options. Kakao Mobility Collaborates With NVIDIA to Advance Autonomous Driving Development Kakao Mobility plans to build on NVIDIA’s autonomous vehicle computing and safety technologies to advance development of a level 4 autonomous driving system. The work combines Kakao Mobility’s proprietary driving software and experience operating in Seoul’s Gangnam district with NVIDIA’s vehicle computing platform. Kakao Mobility plans to use NVIDIA Hyperion , a reference platform for vehicle sensors and compute, powered by NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor. It also plans to use NVIDIA Halos to support safety across the development and validation of its autonomous driving technology. Initial development is planned around Kia purpose-built vehicles, integrating Kakao Mobility’s autonomous driving software with NVIDIA technologies. The effort aims to support future level 4 mobility services in Korea. LG Electronics Advances Robot Learning and Factory Simulation NVIDIA and LG Electronics successfully demonstrated NVIDIA Isaac GR00T-powered robotic manipulation and manufacturing tasks using LG’s CLOiD robot in an actual manufacturing environment. The collaboration implemented a physical AI data flywheel connecting real-world data collection, NVIDIA Cosmos-based data augmentation, GR00T model training, NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor onboard computing and simulation-based evaluation, establishing reusable workflows for continued development and validation of CLOiD’s robotic capabilities. The teams are using this work to refine a repeatable process for training, evaluating and improving robots for manufacturing.

articles.title: Korea’s AI Ecosystem Advances and Secures Agentic AI With NVIDIA
articles.content: As AI agents take on more work, they need capable open models and security that advances alongside them. Hyundai Motor Group is exploring NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and the NVIDIA OpenShell runtime, while AIM Intelligence is integrating its Starfort platform with NVIDIA OpenShell to support secure AI agents for employee productivity and enterprise workflows . A key component of the NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform, OpenShell provides a secure runtime with sandboxed execution and policy-based controls to safeguard sensitive data, manage access to enterprise tools and govern autonomous agent actions. AIM Intelligence , a Korean AI security company, is integrating its Starfort agent control platform with NVIDIA OpenShell. The goal is to combine OpenShell’s runtime access controls with Starfort’s detection of malicious instructions and data leakage. The company is also considering a preliminary proof of concept for the public energy sector, with potential applications across enterprise, industrial and robotics environments. On the model side, LG AI Research is opening application programming interface access for K-EXAONE-2.5, developed using NVIDIA Nemotron datasets, including Nemotron-Personas-Korea . Nemotron-Personas-Korea is an open dataset of 7 million fully synthetic Korean personas, grounded in official Korean statistics, that model builders use to ground training data and evaluation in Korean contexts. NVIDIA Nemotron is a family of open models, datasets and techniques that help developers build specialized, efficient AI agents. Learn more about NVIDIA Nemotron open models and get started building secure agents with NVIDIA OpenShell .

articles.title: From Chips to Skills, NVIDIA and Korea Expand Sovereign AI Collaboration
articles.content: NVIDIA and Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) are expanding their collaboration across the country’s sovereign AI ecosystem, from AI semiconductors and data center infrastructure to talent, startups, models, agents and security. The collaboration lays the groundwork for Korean NPU and XPU companies to explore participation in the NVIDIA NVLink Fusion ecosystem, and includes NVIDIA training and certification programs, hackathons and technical seminars to strengthen GPU utilization. Through Korea’s AI for All initiative, NVIDIA will collaborate with three selected consortia and four leading Korean foundation model builders, using NVIDIA Dynamo software to optimize and scale AI inference. In addition, NVIDIA today announced a collaboration with SK Telecom and Rebellions, supported by MSIT, to advance sovereign AI infrastructure for Korean models and workloads with NVIDIA NVLink Fusion. Read more in the press release .

articles.title: NVIDIA Dynamo Recipes Bring Korea’s Leading Open Models to Production
articles.content: NVIDIA is releasing Dynamo-optimized deployment recipes for Korea’s leading open models: A.X K2 from SK Telecom , K-EXAONE 2.0 from LG AI Research , Solar Open 2 from Upstage and Motif-3 from Motif Technologies . As models grow beyond the capacity of a single GPU, they must be split across multiple GPUs, requiring careful coordination of request routing and communication to maintain performance. NVIDIA Dynamo is an open source, distributed inference-serving framework built to deploy models in multi-node environments at data center scale. It handles this routing and communication to maximize inference performance. Optimized for NVIDIA B200 GPUs, these recipes take the guesswork out of deployment, delivering up to 2x performance out of the box. They help developers bring Korea’s open models into production faster and turn them into broadly accessible AI for All services. Learn more about NVIDIA Dynamo .

articles.title: A single AI model simulates the behavior of many substances, from sliding sand to folding proteins
articles.content: Today, a scientist who wants to simulate a physical process must pick the right tool for that one job, such as a solver built for flowing water or another designed to model the way a protein folds. Each one is hand-coded around the specific equations that dictate how that process behaves. Researchers at MIT, the University of British Columbia (UBC), and elsewhere have now replaced that patchwork with a single deep-learning system, called WorldParticle , that could help engineers model different physical phenomena, from sliding sand to folding proteins, with one unified artificial intelligence architecture. Scientists and engineers could use this system to model processes that typically require separate simulators, such as a fluid sloshing against a deformable solid. This could offer a faster, more accurate way to simulate how sloshing oil might impact an elastic valve in a storage tank, for instance. It could also help engineers study where and how granular materials, like sand or soil, could move when a soft robot touches them. The system represents every material it simulates, from a dune of sand to a protein molecule, as tiny particles and predicts where those particles will move one step at a time. Because it learns the underlying dynamics rather than being programmed with an equation, the model can adapt to materials, forces, and environments it never encountered during training. In the long term, the researchers hope this work helps scientists discover new materials and explore physical processes they would be unable to effectively study with existing simulation methods. “We want to have a GPT moment for simulation,” says Peter Yichen Chen, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at UBC, and is a co-corresponding author of an open-access paper on this technique. “Every time people want to build a simulator for a particular physical phenomenon, they need to code it up from scratch. Our vision is to have a foundation model that works out of the box for any scenario you want to simulate. This is a first step in that direction.” Chen is joined by co-corresponding and co-lead author Minghao Guo, an MIT postdoc; co-lead authors Caoliwen Wang and Siyuan Chen, UBC graduate students; Wojciech Matusik, an MIT professor of electrical engineering and computer science who leads the Computational Design and Fabrication Group within the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL); and others at UBC, Georgia Tech, Inria, Meta, the University of Pennsylvania, the University of Utah, the University of California at Los Angeles, and the University of Hong Kong. The research will be presented at the ACM SIGGRAPH Conference and Exhibition on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques in Asia. Unified simulation For this work, the researchers drew inspiration from world models. These powerful AI systems learn the rules that govern the physical world so they can predict how objects or environments will change over time in response to certain actions or conditions. The researchers applied these concepts to develop a unified AI architecture that can simulate multiple types of physical phenomena. “If you study deformable objects and fluids, you would need two simulators — one for each physical regime. But if you unify them into one model, maybe you could couple the physics of these two processes and gain insights into new problems?” Guo says. WorldParticle breaks an object into thousands or millions of tiny, three-dimensional dots, or particles, using what is known as a Lagrangian representation. It tracks the movement and velocity of the particles over space and time to simulate the material’s dynamics. Typically, when scientists model materials and physical processes using Lagrangian particles, they use a governing equation that defines the fundamental laws which control how that material behaves over time and space. articles.title: AI-assisted learning platform helps robots reason beyond literal commands
articles.content: Humans are intuitive by nature. We can sense meaning beyond the literal words that we encounter. Now, a new artificial intelligence-assisted learning platform developed by MIT engineers is enabling robots to read larger meaning into a human’s natural language commands. In a study to be presented at the annual Conference on Robot Learning this month, researchers from MIT and New York University introduce FLEX , a flexible feature-editing pipeline for robot motion-planning. With FLEX, humans can interact with a robot by giving it instructions in natural, conversational language. The robot can not only follow the instructions literally but also read into the words to draw larger generalizations that help to improve its motion-planning task. The team demonstrated FLEX in several simulated scenarios, including one in which a robot serves a cup of coffee. In these virtual scenarios, a person interacts with a robotic arm by typing commands in natural language. As the robot moves the coffee cup over a cluttered table, the person might type “Don’t spill on the laptop!” In response, the robot will reason about why it should avoid the laptop. For this, FLEX incorporates a large language model (LLM) — a type of AI system that is trained on enormous libraries of text, including social media posts, video transcriptions, and web content, which the LLM uses to identify larger trends, patterns, and generalizations. “LLMs have seen so many texts from the internet,” says study author Nathan Dennler, a postdoc in MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). “People might have written about, ‘Oh, my phone dropped in the water and now it doesn’t work,’ or ‘I spilled coffee on my computer and now it doesn’t work.’ So LLMs pick up on the idea that liquids plus devices leads to things not working.” Through the LLM, the robot reasons that it should also avoid bumping into all electronics. In its updated path, the robot adjusts to avoid both the laptop and a nearby phone, without the person having to explicitly spell this out. “The idea is that there is some higher-level intention behind the words that you say,” Dennler says. “People naturally get this. But you have to carefully explain that to a robot, which takes time and effort. FLEX gives you an interface of communication with a robot to say, ‘When people say this, they mean that.’” The study was led by Andreea Bobu, assistant professor of aeronautics and astronautics at MIT. Co-authors are Audrey Lee SM ’26 and Ilia Sucholutsky of New York University. Beyond what we say At MIT, Bobu heads up the Collaborative Learning and Autonomy Research (CLEAR) Lab, where her group develops autonomous agents that learn to work for, with, and around people. She is focused on developing assistive and household robots that can carry out physical tasks, and reason and adapt in real-time, in response to a person’s natural, conversational commands. “Robots use math to do their trajectory planning. But we can’t expect a consumer to learn to do this math in order to tell a robot what to do,” says Dennler, who is a member of the CLEAR Lab. “Instead of having to get people to learn how to use a robot in a specific way, the goal is to interact with the robot through natural language.” There is a large effort in the robotics community to incorporate natural language into robotic learning pipelines. Various strategies include using language to clarify a task’s goal, redirect a robot’s trajectory, and update its understanding of what is a safe path to take. These existing methods use natural language to tell the robot how to physically perform a task. But a robot could potentially learn much more from what we tell it. Bobu and her colleagues are expanding what robots can learn from natural language commands. articles.title: Linus Torvalds sees signs AI-prompted patch flood has peaked
articles.content: The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds. Writing in his weekly kernel update post , the Linux kernel dev leader delivered Linux 7.4 rc2 – the second rough cut of the next kernel – which he rated as a big release for two reasons. One is that he left some code out of rc1, because he was busy and because it was already the largest such release in the history of the kernel. The other is what Torvalds described as “various AI fixes.” Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April , developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible. Microsoft, for example, addressed a record 974 flaws in September – its third record fixing spree this year after it whacked 622 flaws in July and 206 in June. Oracle addressed 1,449 flaws in a single month. That’s many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI . Torvalds’ post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us. “This time around Alexei claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true,” he wrote. That’s a reference to Alexei Starovoitov, co-creator and lead dev on the Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), the project that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs within the Linux kernel. “I think most other areas haven't reached that point yet, but it's at least a sign that we _may_ be starting to see the tide starting to turn,” he added. “Don't hold your breath, but maybe cross your fingers we'll be getting there in the not entirely distant future.” If Torvalds is correct, that’s welcome news. The Linux kernel’s 40-million-plus lines of code makes it one of the world’s bigger software projects. If AI soon stops finding flaws in other parts of the kernel beyond eBPF, perhaps the deluge of fixes developers and users alike will need to handle has peaked. ®

articles.title: Apple Store Subscription Sign-Up Controversy Exposed
articles.content: In a series of YouTube videos shared over the past two weeks, electronics technician and consumer rights advocate Louis Rossmann has exposed a controversy in which some Apple Store employees have allegedly signed up customers for auto-renewing subscription trials for Apple One and other services without their informed consent. Here is how the process works at Apple Stores in the United States: A customer visits an Apple Store. An employee at the store asks if the customer would like to scan a QR code for a personalized shopping experience ("Connect and Personalize"). If the customer agrees, the employee can view some of the customer's information on their company-issued device, including which Apple devices they own, which Apple services they are subscribed to, and which Apple subscription offers are available to them based on their recent purchases. The employee can proceed to show the customer their available subscription offers, presented with "Agree" and "Decline" buttons on the employee's device. The default payment method associated with the customer's Apple Account is automatically available for subscription sign-ups, so long as it has not expired. The problem is that some employees allegedly activated these trials without adequately explaining to the customers that they would be automatically charged at a later date, according to tipsters who contacted Rossmann. For example, some employees would allegedly rush through the process or were even told to position the trials as "gifts." Until early last week, Apple was tracking a metric known as the "services attach rate," with a target of 40% for each retail employee at at least some U.S. stores. In other words, employees were encouraged to get at least four out of every 10 customers they assisted with a device purchase to also sign up for at least one subscription. In some cases, employees allegedly even tapped the "Agree" button themselves without receiving the customer's informed consent, seemingly in an attempt to ensure that their "services attach rate" was as high as possible. Apple does email customers when a new trial has been activated on their accounts, but unsuspecting customers might not pay attention or realize that the email pertains to a subscription that will automatically renew later. Metric Removed, Reminder Issued MacRumors has confirmed that Apple removed the services metric for employees early last week, just days after Rossmann's videos were published. However, the official explanation we were given for the metric's removal is that it is less relevant during the holiday season, when customers are often purchasing Apple products as gifts for others. Later in the week, Apple issued an internal memo to retail employees reminding them of the importance of respecting customer privacy and obtaining consent, including when offering subscription trials and using the "Connect and Personalize" system, but also for things such as Apple Upgrade sign-ups and Genius Bar work authorizations. The memo was issued ahead of the first weekend of Apple's holiday shopping season, which kicked off on Friday . During the holidays, Apple hires additional employees to help assist with an influx of customers, so the reminder was timely for new staff. Whether these actions were timed solely around the holiday shopping season or were also influenced by Rossmann's videos, we cannot say for sure. In any case, the actions conveniently address some of the concerns highlighted by Rossmann. How to Check Your Subscriptions On an iPhone, open the Settings app and tap on your name at the top of the screen. Next, tap on "Subscriptions" and you will see a list of any subscriptions that are active on your Apple Account, including trials. You can tap on any individual subscription and tap on the "Cancel Subscription" or "Cancel All Services" button to cancel. If you wish to dispute a transaction with Apple, go to reportaproblem.apple.com , select the "Request a refund" option, and follow the…

articles.title: Electric Cars Are Close to Overtaking Petrol In the UK, Data Shows
articles.content: 69 million people people live in the United Kingdom. And now >Electrek reports: Battery-electric cars took 32% of the UK's new car market in October, while petrol cars fell to just 37.2%, according to new data from the SMMT. That's the closest the two have been. At the current pace, electric cars will outsell petrol in the UK within a year. And it could happen as soon as this December. The UK registered 152,730 new cars in October, up 5.4% year-over-year and the 11th straight month of growth for the overall market. All of that growth came from plug-ins. Battery-electric vehicle registrations jumped 32.7% to 48,858 units, and plug-in hybrids rose 30.1% to 22,898. Meanwhile, petrol fell 11.6% to 56,876 units, diesel dropped 15.9%, and even conventional hybrids were down 5%... The brands growing fastest in the UK are mostly Chinese. BYD registered 6,065 cars in October, up 73%. Jaecoo more than doubled to 6,089 units, Chery nearly tripled to 3,707, and Leapmotor doubled to 1,773. MG was up 85%. Looking at trend lines, EV car sales surpass petrol sales "around August 2027 at roughly 33% each," the article points out. "But that's the slow scenario, because it ignores December." UK battery-electric vehicle share spikes every December as automakers push volume to get closer to their zero-emission vehicle mandate targets... Petrol's days as the UK's default car are numbered. The only question is whether the milestone comes in December or sometime in 2027. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
