articles.title: Inside Viggle Remake: LoRA-Based Video Editing With MiniMax-H3
articles.content: Overview Viggle Remake is a video-to-video editing model built from rank-256 LoRA adapters on MiniMax-H3. It supports character replacement as well as broader edits to objects, backgrounds, weather, lighting, and style. The maintainer is Viggle . Best use cases Use it to recast people or characters, change outfits, add or remove objects, and alter a video's setting, weather, lighting, or style while retaining source motion, camera, timing, and soundtrack. The repository describes both single-shot use and workflows that split longer films into windows. Limitations The reference sampler handles one window of about 12 seconds; longer videos require windowing, which the MCP workflow can perform. The base MiniMax-H3 files total about 144 GB, and the reference sampler requires the base text encoder and one GPU with at least 80 GB memory at bf16; ComfyUI alternatives are documented for smaller cards. A six-section prompt is required, and timestamps must fit the requested frame count. Painted reference frames determine identity and appearance; pinned frames also constrain composition. Audio is carried from the source rather than generated. Documented failure cases include non-humanoid characters in a long take, fine-detail artifacts, and timing drift in multi-shot clips rendered without pins. The model cannot verify identity or consent; use footage and likenesses only with appropriate rights and consent, and label generated content as AI-generated. How it compares Viggle-Animate is described as replacing a character, while Remake also supports object insertion or removal and changes to setting, weather, and lighting. Viggle-Animate is the supplied internal alternative. Other supplied alternatives include LTX-2 Retake , Luma Ray 3.2 Reframe , Ray2 Flash Modify , and Luma Modify Video ; the supplied descriptions do not establish a quality, speed, or cost ranking. The README identifies Remake as the “Viggle-Animate v2” previewed on the Viggle-Animate card; that is a version relationship, not evidence that the separate Animate model has Remake's full feature set. Technical specifications The model consists of two PEFT LoRA adapters, swap and edit , each rank 256 and about 2.67 GB, applied to the MiniMax-H3 base transformer. Lower-rank variants at ranks 128 and 64 are also provided, at about 1.34 GB and 0.67 GB respectively; the README describes their output as near-identical. The required base files are about 144 GB. The repository also contains ComfyUI assets and merged int8 and GGUF transformers. The reference sampler uses bf16 and requires an 80 GB-or-larger GPU. It renders at 24 fps, with frame counts from 90 to 345 following 17n + 5 ; the README recommends up to 294 frames. At short edge 736, the documented output size is 1280×736. No training data, training procedure, or measured benchmark results are supplied. The weights are derivatives of MiniMax-H3 and are subject to the MiniMax H3 Community License; the supplied code directories are Apache 2.0. Model inputs and outputs Inputs The reference sampler takes a source video, a prompt in MiniMax-H3's six-section format, and one to four painted reference images. Each reference can optionally be pinned to the source frame it was painted from. Select swap to replace people or characters, or edit for other edits such as object changes and background, weather, or lighting changes. The prompt's timestamps must fit the selected frame count. The sampler accepts a seed and short-edge setting; ffmpeg must be available on PATH. Outputs The sampler produces a rendered video window and carries over the source soundtrack; it does not generate audio, so silent input produces silent output. The MCP workflow can split a longer video into windows and splice the rendered results with the soundtrack. The README documents 24 fps output and a 1280×736 size when --short-edge 736 is used. articles.title: Trevor Noah on AI
articles.content: Trevor Noah, Rana el Kaliouby and Oren Etzioni discuss AI onstage at Boston’s Museum of Science on Oct. 19. (Nicolaus Czarnecki Photography for the Museum of Science, Boston) On Oct. 19, Trevor Noah launched Luminaries , a science conversation series at Boston’s Museum of Science. I joined him onstage, and Rana el Kaliouby moderated. Rana is a pioneer of emotion AI, software that reads human emotion, and the host of the Pioneers of AI podcast . She wrote afterward that she expected Trevor to be witty and funny, but “didn’t expect to be so blown away by his humanity and depth of ideas.” Here are a few of his insights with his own words highlighted. AI often appears deep but merely works on the surface When an AI matchmaker Rana built in ChatGPT picked Trevor as her match, he pointed out that it knew very little about either of them. It assembled a plausible answer from what’s on the internet. “AI is particularly good at seeming like it has gone beneath the surface, when in fact it’s calculating everything above the surface.” Trevor added that when you tell AI it made a mistake, it thanks you but often fails to correct the error: “It’s like a friend who’s been to a lot of therapy but doesn’t actually change.” In-person community is a defense against a dystopian AI future When asked how we protect ourselves from AI’s downsides, Trevor said the answer “goes back to something that is very un-technological and very un-AI.” He cited Robert Putnam’s book Bowling Alone , noting that places where communities form accrue many surprising benefits including more accountable governments. I pushed back that communitarianism , the 1990s movement my father helped found to foster communities, had failed. Trevor responded that we hand too many ideas to intellectuals, who then “apply too much academia” to them. Communitarianism failed, he deadpanned, “because it’s called communitarianism.” An overly academic name. He noted that nobody calls a phone a failure when the first version doesn’t sell; companies keep re-releasing it. He vowed never to stop investing in community. “I don’t need to see if you’re a deepfake, because I’m sitting here with you.” Trevor is optimistic about technology Despite his concerns, Trevor has “yet to see a technology that blew up and then left everyone behind.” Cars, computers and the internet all spread to ordinary people. AI has reached what he calls “work intelligence”: it can do the jobs we invented, but we keep inventing new ones. Salt and ice used to be precious. Now restaurants hand them out for free. What we value changes, and in Trevor’s view, we’re expendable only if we define being human by the tasks we value today. “If we are the people who draw pictures of ourselves on a cave wall, and we sing songs for no reason really, then we’re infinitely capable as creatures.” Our conversation turned to AI’s impact on jobs. The real jobs question is the following distance Touring as a comic, Trevor saw towns hollowed out after Kodak and the automaker Studebaker left. Factory workers were told automation was progress. “White-collar workers are now experiencing what many blue-collar workers experienced for decades,” he said. The difference, he argued, is that white-collar workers are closer to power, so newspapers are covering it. Trevor is confident new jobs will come, as they did after telephone exchange operators disappeared. What worries him is the gap. His analogy is the highway, where the following distance is the space that lets you stop before you hit the car ahead: “There is no job that will last forever. There is nothing that won’t be displaced. The question is, how long is the following distance between the two things?” Trevor tells tech leaders that “it’s easier to be patient when you are in a position of privilege,” and added, “But ironically, they don’t have patience when it comes to quarterly earnings.” Why AI isn’t coming for Trevor’s job After ChatGPT took off, show hosts kept telling him weak…

articles.title: Do Data Centers Have a Smaller Effect on Electricity Prices Than We Think?
articles.content: "According to a new study by researchers at Harvard University and the University of Pennsylvania, data centers are probably having only a small effect on residential electricity prices," reports the Washington Post. "The researchers calculated that these operations were responsible for just 4% of the utility rate increases over the last five years..." There are certainly some areas — like in Pennsylvania, Virginia, Ohio and other states covered by grid operator PJM — where data centers have skyrocketed demand, pushing some costs onto residential customers. But multiple studies by different researchers and organizations have failed to find a strong connection between data centers and the overall trajectory of U.S. electricity prices in recent years. Another analysis earlier this year by researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology found that, between 2010 and 2024, data centers increased average electricity prices for residential customers by just 2.1%. Last year, research from the Brattle Group and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found that data centers were actually decreasing costs in certain regions. And another study by the Electric Power Research Institute found that a doubling of data center capacity between 2019 and 2024 resulted in a 4 percent drop in home electricity prices... The new Harvard and Penn study found a slightly higher impact on industrial electricity prices — the price paid by manufacturers and large facilities. For those customers, data centers were responsible for 15% of the price increase between 2020 and 2025. But for ordinary Americans... the changes simply were not substantial [according to Wharton School professor Serguei Netessine, one of the study's authors]. "So far we have no evidence that data centers increase prices all that much," Netessine said. Instead, he said, prices are rising due to more quotidian factors: rising gas prices, an aging electricity grid, and wildfires and hurricanes requiring improvements to the grid and recovery after disaster... If the number of data centers continue to boom, experts say, residential prices could be affected more down the line. Data center electricity demand is expected to increase steeply over the next few years, requiring new power generation — wind, solar or natural gas — to be put onto the grid. And residents have issues with data centers that go beyond the price of electricity. The new developments have been singled out for loud noise, polluting power generation, and for disturbing residential neighborhoods and natural landscapes. According to the Pew Research Center, more than half of Americans say that data centers are mostly bad for the environment. Others feel that the AI race — which could ultimately leave many Americans out of work — is being forced upon them. "I think generally what we're seeing is a broader range of reasons the public has opposed data centers," [said Ryan Hledik, principal at the Brattle Group]. "Concern about AI leading to loss of jobs — all of that is getting packaged together." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Siri AI Rumored to Become 'More Like an Agent' as Early as Next Year
articles.content: Siri AI is much more intelligent and personalized compared to classic Siri, but it is still not nearly as advanced as proactive, always-on agents like OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse. That may change, though, according to a new rumor. In his Power On newsletter today , Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman said he was told that Apple could make Siri function "more like an agent" as early as next year. However, if this plan moves forward, the exact implementation remains to be seen. "Dots, Muse and Grok can keep track of goals, determine what needs to happen next and continue pursuing objectives without the user initiating every individual step," said Gurman. "Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I'm told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year." Apple's AI ambitions could go beyond making Siri more agentic. In a closed-door meeting in recent weeks, Gurman said that Apple CEO John Ternus told Apple's software engineering chief Craig Federighi that Apple needs to "accelerate" its software roadmap and "move quickly beyond merely making necessary improvements to Siri." articles.title: Google and Microsoft among those signing up to OpenAI's plan for a new website crawling standard — including opting-out of internet scraping
articles.content: Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic say they will honor one robots.txt group as a cross-company opt-out from AI training It governs how content is used rather than whether bots can crawl it, defaults to allowing training, and does nothing for content already scraped Anthropic has started implementing it, OpenAI promises to do so in the coming months, Microsoft starts February 1, 2027, and Google targets 2027, while Meta is supportive but uncommitted Google and Microsoft have joined OpenAI and Anthropic in promising to honor a single line in robots.txt that tells AI developers whether a website's content can be used to train their models. Until now, a site that wanted to say no had to write a rule for each company's crawler, and sometimes for several crawlers run by the same company. The shared signal is meant to replace that sprawl with a single entry that every participating provider reads the same way. That is genuine progress for overworked webmasters, but the promise is narrower than much of the coverage suggests: The new line states a preference about how content may be used rather than stopping bots from fetching it; it is not an approved standard, does nothing about content already collected, and none of the four major players fully honor it yet. Doing the bare minimum with differing definitions of what the commitment entails OpenAI's announcement drew much of the attention, but the company casts itself as one participant among several in an Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) effort, and the mechanism isn't its own. It comes from an Internet-Draft published the same day by Kevin Kelley of Anthropic, which names a policy token, "__usage_ai-training", in the User-Agent line of an otherwise ordinary robots.txt group. Training is defined by the IETF's AI Preferences (AIPREF) working group as the process of changing a generative model's learned parameters, excluding models used purely for tasks such as classification or ranking. OpenAI describes what it will honor as "foundational generative AI training," which sounds narrower than the draft's definition. Calling it a standard may be premature: The IETF's own tracker labels the document an individual draft that the IETF has not endorsed, and that has no formal standing, and it lapses on May 3, 2027 unless revised. Anthropic is the only one of the four major AI players to say it has started. OpenAI aims to implement the signal over the next few months but has given no date. Microsoft will begin honoring the shared preference as it crawls from February 1, 2027, while Google is aiming for 2027. Each company is also wiring the line into its own controls differently. Google says that when a site uses the shared token to opt out without separately specifying Google-Extended, it plans to treat that "as if the publisher had disallowed Google-Extended." Because Google-Extended also governs grounding in Gemini Apps, a site that only wants to stop training could lose its citations and clicks in Gemini answers too, and Search Engine Journal notes that Google's documentation describes no way to separate the two. Interestingly, Microsoft goes the other way. It adopts the shared line for training but adds a separate, page-level AI Grounding preference, including a DisallowExtended option that keeps content available to its own products such as Copilot while excluding the grounding services it sells to other businesses. Meta, not one of the four, has been warmer than it has been about its commitment. Its VP of communications, Andy Stone, called the common signal "an important step," but SiliconANGLE reports the company has not committed to honoring it. The timing is awkward: Meta has pushed back to November 20 revised commercial terms that would let it crawl websites linked to its business accounts, after a backlash forced it to strip training from the listed uses. With training removed but not expressly banned, Sam Quigley of the News/Media Alliance told the Mercury News last…

articles.title: Marketers Are BURNED OUT -  And No One Gives AF
articles.content: I have read countless posts about bloated marketing roles where six jobs are crammed into one title. One listing asked for a “Marketing Manager” to handle brand strategy, paid media, SEO, email marketing, copywriting, and front-end web design. All of that... on a junior salary! These are not rare. They are the norm these days. Scroll LinkedIn or Reddit for five minutes and you will see post after post of people venting about being stretched thin, underpaid, and told to be “grateful for the opportunity.” I have been reading these for a YEAR now. Watching the same story play out. Marketers are asking, “Is it just me, or has marketing completely lost the plot? Is this the job I wanted? Should I just switch careers?” I even asked the same things myself. I used to love marketing. Now, I don't even know what to say. What even was marketing before all of this? Was it always like this and we are just noticing it now? Or did it get worse in the last few years? What used to be a blend of strategy and execution turned into survival mode . AI promised efficiency. Instead, it created more expectation. Faster turnarounds. More output. Tighter budgets. Leadership sees AI as a shortcut, not a tool. So the workload? It went up. Headcount? Went down. Pressure? TRIPLED. The marketer role did not evolve. It got gutted and repackaged. This article is not about the trends. Not the hype. Just focusing on the one question we all dread to be answered. How real is marketer burnout, and how did we get here? What happens when your creative energy gets consumed by meetings, client briefs, and endless edits? How do you stay motivated when everyone blames your team for poor performance but no one credits you when a campaign wins? Why do marketers, especially in digital, feel like they are always running on empty? The Modern Marketing Role is a Trap! Burnout in marketing is not new. What’s different now is how fast it spreads and how deeply it affects people across roles. From content specialists and media buyers to strategists and SEO managers, burnout is everywhere. Not because people are lazy or bad at their jobs. They are overwhelmed, underappreciated, and stuck in systems that demand more while offering less. Marketers today wear too many hats. Generalist roles stretch across brand, analytics, operations, and sales support. It used to be enough to run great creative. Now you are expected to prove ROI, optimize in real-time, adjust to AI tools, and still produce on-brand messaging across ten platforms. The second something underperforms, marketing takes the fall. But when results are good? Sales or other department will take the credit. That’s not an exaggeration. One Reddit comment I saw earlier hit it perfectly: “The sales team shouldn't be the only ones getting commission since we (content team) did all the work.” That’s the norm in many agencies and in-house teams. Marketers drive interest, create value, and nurture leads. Sales closes once the hard part is already done. There’s a word for that dynamic: exhausting . The Workload Keeps Growing Burnout is tied to more than just being busy. It’s the layoffs. The increased cost of living. The consolidation of roles. Managers freeze raises. Employees fear losing their jobs, so they overperform to avoid the next round of cuts. That creates a cycle. You take on more . You work harder . You don’t complain . And then your reward is more responsibility, not more support. Not a better salary. You become your own bottleneck. You say yes to everything because the team is small and leadership needs “just one more push.” Eventually, you hit a wall. Creativity dies. Enthusiasm fades. Work turns into survival. No Respect, No Boundaries Marketing roles are highly visible but rarely respected. Everyone thinks they can do your job. Leadership gives vague direction but expects strong positioning. Product teams shift priorities mid-sprint. Sales wants new decks with impossible turnaround times. People expect you to spin…

articles.title: Moving from AI adoption to an AI operating model: How Docusign engineering went beyond tool rollout
articles.content: Docusign rolled out AI coding tools across its engineering teams, expecting them to help developers write code faster and do more. Initial enthusiasm was high, but early gains plateaued. By June 2025, Docusign had reached a sticking point. According to its engineering team’s account , 49% of engineers were actively using AI coding tools, while a reported 18% improvement in developer productivity had leveled off. Engineers still needed time to experiment, guidance tailored to Docusign’s codebase, and help fitting the tools into their day-to-day work. Docusign now reports that all of its more than 1,100 engineers are onboarded to and actively using AI coding tools Docusign CTO Sagnik Nandy CTO Sagnik Nandy believes getting people to use the technology is only the beginning. “There’s a big difference between trying to get a few wins versus doing it consistently and doing it right,” Nandy tells The New Stack . Docusign responded by changing how it introduced and measured AI across engineering, moving beyond coding assistants toward reusable agents and automated workflows. Why Docusign turned to its engineers Instead of making AI adoption mandatory, Docusign established a six-person Eng AI Champions team to develop guardrails, share engineering practices, and run workshops. Docusign reports that adoption reached 65% by October 2025. The company then extended that work through AI Multipliers embedded in individual development teams. Nandy says around 75 Multipliers helped teammates put the shared practices into use and fed problems back to the central team. “They were tasked with two things,” Nandy explains. “The decisions, the solutions we built, they had to deploy it within their team, and also get feedback in terms of what’s working, what’s not working, and what’s missing.” Docusign’s account of the initiative showed that active usage reached 93% within two months of introducing the Multipliers, while lines of code updated per developer increased by approximately 52% from the company’s starting point. That code-volume measure does not, by itself, establish a matching improvement in delivery speed or software quality. Nandy believes the combination of central coordination and feedback from individual teams has helped sustain the program, an approach he has also discussed in an engineering leadership podcast . “When I speak to many of my peers, a lot of AI programs start well, and then fizzle out.” “When I speak to many of my peers, a lot of AI programs start well, and then fizzle out,” he says. “I think the reason that hasn’t happened for us … is because we already have such a rich body of information and feedback flowing in, and people acting on it and then redeploying things.” Teaching AI to ‘speak Docusign’ Once engineers were comfortable using AI for coding, Docusign began looking at entire development workflows. That required tools with access to its repositories, architecture, telemetry, and internal practices, so assistants could work with the company’s own context. “Our solutions and agents, we joke, they speak Docusign,” Nandy says. “They know which internal tools to go look into, what our internal coding guardrails are, guidelines are, what system choices we make, where information resides for disambiguating between different pieces of information.” Nandy describes several internal tools for different engineering tasks: Kody for Docusign-specific coding work, Chronicle for observability and incident investigation, and DocuWiki for code-aware internal documentation. Docusign’s engineering blog also describes an AI-assisted code review tool for identifying potential architectural and security issues during review. Krew brings these capabilities together , allowing teams to build agents called Krewmates for recurring tasks and more complex…

articles.title: I took the iPhone 18 Pro to New Zealand to find out just how good its cameras really are
articles.content: Apple has touted the addition of a variable aperture main camera on the new iPhone 18 Pro , claiming it delivers an improvement in low-light photos and video, and more control over depth of field when composing shots. But with an almost identical design and spec sheet to the excellent iPhone 17 Pro , the iPhone 18 Pro begs the question: are these camera upgrades incremental, or worth the extra investment? I received my iPhone 18 Pro review sample on September 21, two days before flying to New Zealand for a month-long trip to see family and friends. The country's dramatic scenery proved the perfect place to put the iPhone 18 Pro through its paces, and I ended up shooting more than 750 still images to see if Apple's much-hyped photography upgrades cut the mustard. In addition to that variable aperture feature, Apple also added ‘pro’ manual controls to the iPhone 18 Pro's camera app for the first time, as well as more customization options for Photographic Styles, including a film effect and film grain effect. Cumulatively, these granular control options are quite un-Apple, putting much more control in the hands of an iPhone photographer who might be used to a simpler point-and-shoot experience. In doing so, Apple is asking for its latest iPhone to be held to a higher standard. And the bottom line is that, while the iPhone 18 Pro has the best and most versatile camera setup of any iPhone to date, there are more capable alternatives available just a short hop over the tech fence in Android land for platform-agnostic mobile photographers who want the very best available. Variable aperture (Image credit: Future/Jacob Krol) The variable aperture is a physically moving mechanism that can be manually changed between four different f-stops — the smaller the f-stop number, the more light is allowed to reach the lens, and vice versa. The iPhone 18 Pro’s main camera is a 48MP sensor that can switch between f/1.4, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0. This makes it the most flexible iPhone camera lens to date, but Apple only allows those four settings — unlike a real camera, you can’t adjust to incremental f-stops between those numbers. The variable aperture in action on the iPhone 18 Pro (Image credit: Jacob Krol/Future) Changing the aperture on the iPhone 18 Pro subtly changes how much background blur a shot has when there's a subject in focus in the foreground. This is how cameras work, but usually, the small sensor on a phone requires software-enabled portrait modes to achieve this bokeh effect. The iPhone 18 Pro can do it with hardware only, though the difference between the four settings is quite minimal, as seen here: f/1.48 Future f/1.8 Future f/2.8 Future f/4.0 Future You can change the aperture manually, but it’ll also change automatically by default. And after a month of using the iPhone 18 Pro as my main camera, I feel this is still how Apple's latest flagship should be used: as a point-and-shoot camera with its default settings enabled. As you can see from many of my favorite images, the iPhone chooses the main lens at f/1.8 frequently, and it'll usually be spot on. As mentioned, this variable aperture is the headline feature of the iPhone 18 Pro, but the subtlety with which it changes the photography experience versus the iPhone 17 Pro suggests there’s not much more Apple can do with its flagship camera system. That said, the addition of customizable ‘pro’ controls within the camera app is a nice touch. I set my control panel to show shutter speed, white balance, and aperture, and they were fun to play around with to achieve better shots in low light, for instance. But unless you're invested in wringing the best possible results from the iPhone 18 Pro's lenses, you’ll likely forget about these new controls after a while. The good news is that, if you're a more casual shooter, Tap to Focus continues to work well on the iPhone 18 Pro. I was impressed with the main lens' ability to capture the two images below. articles.title: Netflix just added 15 shows in November 2026 — here are the top 3 with the highest scores on Rotten Tomatoes (all 92% or higher)
articles.content: Netflix’s November 2026 slate is live, and so far this month, the streamer's added a whopping 15 new shows to its library. I'd wager that’s more shows than most subscribers probably watch in a whole year — trying to finish it all in a month is basically impossible. To help you figure out what to watch first, I’ve turned to review site Rotten Tomatoes to pick out the Netflix arrivals with the highest critics' scores. Of course, just because a show has a high Rotten Tomatoes rating doesn't mean it will be to every Netflix subscriber's taste, but it's a great jumping off point to see which new-to-Netflix shows are probably worth your time. Before diving into November's top three, a quick point of order: Any Netflix originals not yet released at the time of writing were left off the list, as they lack Rotten Tomatoes scores. If two titles tied, I used the audience score to break the deadlock. With that out of the way, here are the three TV shows added to Netflix in November 2026 with the highest scores on Rotten Tomatoes. 'Bass X Machina' A badass Black protagonist in a Western steampunk anime? Sign me up. "Bass X Machina" stars Brian Tyree Henry as Bass Reeves, a real-life escaped slave turned groundbreaking lawman whose legacy inspired a Taylor Sheridan show and HBO’s “Watchmen,” among other pieces of pop culture. Showrunner LeSean Thomas ("The Boondocks," "Black Dynamite," "The Legend of Korra") uses his legacy as a jumping off point for a mesmerizing mythos all its own, blending fantastical steampunk westerns with real-life history — and it's cool as shit. In a frontier crawling with vicious outlaws, rogue machines, and supernatural nasties, Bass — whose sporting a cybernetic arm because it's sick af — has his hands full dispensing justice while keeping his family out of the crossfire. He goes on one last job in search of a missing inventor, roving a post-Civil War steampunk America with his sidekick Dana Starr (Tati Gabrielle) in tow. Even if anime isn't usually your thing, I urge you to check this one out. Rotten Tomatoes score: 100% Stream all six episodes of "Bass X Machina" on Netflix now 'North of North' season 2 For a perfect show for the dark winter months, look no further than "North of North." Set in Ice Cove, Nunavut, this breezy sitcom unfolds in Canada's northernmost territory, where there's no shortage of daylight. Season 2 sees Anna Lambe return as Siaja, a young mother still finding her footing after divorcing the town's golden boy. This season, she's ready to give romance another shot, and dives headfirst into the chilly waters of the speed-dating scene. Community remains at the heart of the show as Siaja tries to reconnect with her dad (Jay Ryan) and track down her biological sister. Also throwing a wrench in the works is her new boss, Helen (Mary Lynn Rajskub, aka the unforgettable Chloe from "24"). "North of North" is an easygoing comedy with plenty of heart, some seriously gorgeous scenery, and enough low-stakes drama to keep the pace moving along. Rotten Tomatoes score: 100% Stream both seasons of "North of North" on Netflix now 'Black Doves' season 2 For a more high-octane wintry watch, Keira Knightley is back as the fan-favorite spy-for-hire Helen in season 2 of "Black Doves." Still feeding government secrets to the covert organization Black Doves, and with her husband, Wallace (Andrew Buchan), set to become U.K. prime minister, she teams up with her old friend, Sam (Ben Whishaw), for an even more dangerous mission. When her handler, Mrs. Reed, (Sarah Lancashire), is accused of plotting a coup against the organization, it unearths some fascinating revelations about her past, including a family a connection that proves more deadly than anyone expected. There's plenty of twists and sharp dialogue to keep you invested, but the real appeal comes from Whishaw and Knightley, whose genuine chemistry with one another shines through all the shoot outs and drama you'd expect from a spy thriller. articles.title: iOS Startup Performance in Practice, Part 2: Measuring App Launch Time in Production
articles.content: How to measure startup on real user devices, define trustworthy production percentiles, and use XCTest and Instruments to explain regressions. The easiest way to measure app launch time is to start a stopwatch, open the app, and write down the number. It is also one of the easiest ways to produce a measurement that cannot be reproduced, compared, or trusted. An iOS launch depends on more than the code in the repository. The result changes with the process state, system caches, device model, thermal state, available memory, network behavior, stored user data, app version, and the destination the user is trying to open. Two measurements can both be technically correct while describing different experiences. In Part 1 , we separated cold launch, warm launch, resume, scene creation, and entry points. We also defined three possible endpoints: First Draw, Meaningful Content, and Time to Interactive. Now we can turn that model into a measurement system. This article is the second part of iOS Startup Performance in Practice , a six-part series: Understanding Launch Types and Entry Points Measuring App Launch Time Correctly Finding Bottlenecks from dyld to the First Frame Designing a Scalable Startup Architecture From the First Frame to an Interactive UI Preventing Regressions in Production The goal of this part is not to find a single perfect number. It is to build a production measurement system that describes what real users experience - and then use controlled tests and profiling to explain why that distribution changes. A launch number is meaningless without a measurement contract Suppose one engineer reports a launch time of 1.4 seconds and another reports 2.1 seconds. Before comparing them, we need to know: Did both tests create a new process? Were they cold or warm launches? Was the app opened from the icon or through a link? Did the timer stop at First Draw or when the screen became interactive? Did both runs use the same device and OS version? Was the debugger attached? Did both users have the same local data and authentication state? Was the network real, disabled, or stubbed? Without these answers, the numbers are labels rather than evidence. Let’s start with production metrics. For every launch metric, define a measurement contract : Dimension Example value Population Real user launches of app version `8.24.0` Launch class New-process launch; resume reported separately Entry point Icon, link, notification, and quick action segmented where custom telemetry allows it Start boundary System launch start for MetricKit; first application marker for custom metrics End boundary First Draw for the system metric; Home Interactive for the product metric User segments Signed-out and authenticated users reported separately Technical segments Device performance tier, iOS version, app version, and migration state Aggregation window Seven complete days after the target rollout reaches a stable cohort Reported values Every sample, median, p90, and maximum Data source MetricKit or Organizer for system launch; custom telemetry for product milestones Exclusions Internal builds, synthetic runs, invalid or incomplete milestone sequences This table describes measurement on user devices. There are no fixed test phones, stubbed networks, or XCTest iterations in the production contract. Real device and network diversity are not noise to remove; they are part of the experience we are trying to understand. The first rule of launch measurement is therefore: Define the population and user-visible endpoint before naming the number. Instead of writing “launch time is 1.8 seconds,” write: For production new-process launches of version 8.24.x, Time to First Draw is 1.1 seconds at p50 and 1.8 seconds at p90 across 2.4 million samples. Authenticated users on the lowest device tier have a p90 of 2.6 seconds. articles.title: Building Reliable iOS Apps With AI Agents
articles.content: One year ago I wrote Breaking Free from Xcode: Unlock AI's Full Potential in iOS . At that time, getting an agent to build, run and check an iOS app took a pile of MCP servers, VS Code extensions and some patience. A lot has changed since. Models are much smarter. Xcode ships with agents built in. Claude Code can control the simulator on its own: it builds, launches, taps through screens and checks the result with screenshots. So, is iOS development solved? For prototypes and MVPs , mostly yes. You can describe an idea and get the app “one-shotted”. But if your software has to be as reliable as running water (a phrase I borrow from Uber's mission : "transportation as reliable as running water, everywhere, for everyone"), two principles still matter: design and harness . Principle 1: You still own the design This is the biggest shift I've seen. While building a feature, I don't keep in my head which method calls which method, which file it lives in, or how state moves through each type. The agent handles that. That doesn't mean you can stop reviewing code. Where quality matters, you still read PRs. But your attention moves up a level. You own the design of the whole system , not just one module, so architecture is now the most valuable skill you have. At the design level you are pretty high in the hierarchy of components, that’s why visualization helps. A diagram with the right amount of detail shows how the pieces fit together, which is hard to see in plain text. The C4 model gives you that visualization at a few zoom levels. Last year I suggested putting the project architecture in AGENTS.md . I've changed my mind: a dedicated docs/architecture/ folder is a better place. You don't need the entire architecture loaded into the context every time you do something. Instead, AGENTS.md keeps a reference to docs/architecture/context.md , so the agent can retrieve it when on demand. Luis Herrera's deep dive walks through C4 levels on a sample system. System Context. Your app, its users and the outside systems it talks to: the backend, push notifications, analytics. This is context.md , and it links to the containers. Containers. Conventional C4 container usually stands for a piece of software that can de deployed, like a micro-service or app. I had to adapt the original idea: a container is a feature, a flow or an SDK module, like Feed, Checkout or Networking. containers.md shows how they connect, explains what each one owns and what it may depend on, and links to components where they exist. Components. The parts inside a container. Only draw these for complex areas , like a post composer with drafts, uploads and retries, or a sync engine. A stateless FeedService with a single getFeed() call doesn't need a component diagram. C4 itself says you only need the levels "that add value". Code. No diagrams. Component docs just link to the specific files. The code is the source of truth, and an agent can read it faster than you can draw it. Think about C4 as a pattern that generalizes an approach to structure progressive complexity of the architecture. Here's what that looks like for a simple feed app: AGENTS.md ← rules + link to context.md docs/architecture/ context.md ← system context, links to containers.md containers.md ← container diagram, links to components components/composer.md ← complex flow only, links to code Here's the container diagram from containers.md , as Mermaid source and rendered: Use Mermaid. It's plain text, so it shows up in diffs, GitHub renders it, and agents read it as easily as code. This is what I call discoverable architecture . The agent doesn't load the whole architecture up front. AGENTS.md points it to context.md , and from there it follows links down only as far as the task needs. Humans onboard the same way. Keep the diagrams alive Documentation that goes stale is worse than none. So let the agent maintain it: Add a skill that updates the affected docs and diagrams in docs/architecture/ after a change. articles.title: Norwegians Release FOSS GNOME Software for Music Recording, Internet Radio, and Cameras
articles.content: ole (Slashdot reader #19,909) writes in about his free, Norwegian open-source music recording studio for GNOME called GarageJam, which he says allows musicians to compose, record, and share original music seamlessly on the Internet. The latest release, GarageJam 8.0.1, is available in C and Python. It records audio immediately to Ogg Vorbis (.ogg) files in the current working directory and lets you edit metadata in .gjxml XML files from a GTK/GNOME wizard — all built on the Gingerblue Recording Studio API. Ole shares links to its IETF GarageJam XML draft and GitHub repositories, and there's also GarageJam Studio, "a commercial music and audio recording app for the World Wide Web written by Aamot Innovation from Norway.". ole is also spreading the word about GNOME Media, which "puts internet radio and your photographs on one OpenStreetMap... built from GNOME Radio 85.0.1." Click a station on the map to listen. Cities with several stations show a count and a menu. Open a folder of pictures or import from a camera. Photos with a GPS position in their EXIF data appear on the map. Double-click a thumbnail to open it. The search box filters the station list and the map together. ole also announces: GPhoto 3.0.1. articles.title: Scaling an autonomous agent from one team to fifty: A serverless-to-container decision framework
articles.content: QA teams shipping complex products generate test failures around the clock. Every failure needs a bug ticket with steps, screenshots, repro rates, and regression labels. The manual process takes 10-15 minutes per failure. Multiply that by 30+ failures per week across a team, and you have burned an entire engineering day on documentation that should be automatic. I built a system to eliminate this entirely. Not a dashboard. Not a notification bot. An autonomous agent that observes test results, makes judgment calls – is this a new bug, a duplicate, or a regression? And takes action without human intervention. It files structured bugs, attaches screenshots, calculates repro rates, detects regressions build-over-build, and notifies the right people. The team just marks FAIL and moves on. The system runs on Lambda today. It works perfectly for one team. But what happens when other teams want it? What happens when you need to serve 10, 50, or 100 teams? That’s where the architectural decisions get interesting – not because Lambda fails, but because the workload characteristics shift into territory where a different tool becomes the better fit. What I built (and why it works) The architecture is elegant: an EventBridge rule triggers a Lambda function every 15 minutes. The function polls the test management API, processes failures through a decision engine (dedup check against DynamoDB, regression detection against previous build results), and files bugs via the JIRA API. Total infrastructure cost: under $5/month. Lambda was the correct choice here for three reasons: Zero operational overhead: No servers, no scaling config, no patching. Deploy and forget. Cost proportional to usage: One team generates ~200 invocations/month. At Lambda pricing, this is effectively free. Fast iteration: The decision engine went through 20+ revisions in the first month. Lambda’s deployment model let me ship changes in seconds. Within weeks of deploying, the system filed more complete and consistent bugs than the team had ever produced manually. Zero missed failures. Regressions caught in minutes instead of days. Status interruptions to QA dropped to zero because anyone could query the system directly via Slack. 8-10 hours per week saved. Other teams have noticed. “Can we have that?” is a recurring question. The answer seems simple – deploy another instance per team. But at scale, the workload characteristics change in ways that shift the architectural decision. The scaling decision Lambda handles single-tenant agentic workloads beautifully. The challenge at multi-tenant scale isn’t that Lambda can’t do it; it’s that the workload characteristics shift: From stateless events to long-running context: A single team’s poll cycle finishes in seconds. But cross-project correlation – “is this the same failure pattern we’re seeing across three teams?” requires analyzing hundreds of results and their relationships in a single pass. That’s a fundamentally different compute profile. From isolated invocations to shared resource contention: When 50 functions trigger on the same EventBridge schedule, they all hit TestRail and JIRA APIs simultaneously. You need centralized rate limiting, connection pooling, and backpressure – patterns that benefit from persistent, shared infrastructure. From single-team to multi-tenant isolation: Each team needs guaranteed resources, network boundaries, and scoped credentials. The isolation model becomes as important as the compute model. Lambda’s recent launches address many of these individually – Managed Instances solve connection persistence, Durable Functions break the 15-minute ceiling for long-running workflows, and Tenant Isolation provides native tenant boundaries. For many multi-tenant workloads, these capabilities narrow the gap significantly. But for this specific workload – long-running agents that need persistent connections, cross-tenant analysis, GPU inference, and namespace-level isolation simultaneously- the decision…

articles.title: Facebook recovery scams use fake FBI profiles
articles.content: You've already lost money to a scam. You're frustrated and probably wondering whether you'll ever see that money again. Then, while scrolling through Facebook, an advertisement appears promising to recover your stolen funds. Suddenly, there's a little hope. Maybe someone out there can actually help. Unfortunately, that moment of hope is exactly what scammers are trying to exploit . One of our loyal CyberGuy followers, Patrick K, recently tipped us off to suspicious fraud recovery advertisements and profiles appearing on Facebook. He shared screenshots of what he was seeing and urged us to warn others. His tip caught our attention, so we decided to dig deeper and contacted Meta about the suspicious accounts and advertisements. After reviewing the examples we provided, Meta confirmed to CyberGuy that it removed the flagged accounts and ads for violating its impersonation policies. The screenshots Patrick shared are especially concerning. One promotes stolen-asset recovery services. Another uses FBI-related imagery and claims to help people navigate the Internet Crime Complaint Center, better known as IC3. Together, they show how convincing these offers can appear. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. WHY IDENTITY THEFT COMES BACK FOR THE SAME PEOPLE The first screenshot Patrick shared shows a Facebook advertisement displayed under the name Adam Molina. The promotional image features a smiling man in a business suit against a purple background. The graphic bears the name "DARKTRACER" and asks whether you've lost assets or funds to scammers. Below that message, the ad promotes services like recovering stolen assets and retrieving hacked cryptocurrency wallets. At the bottom, there's a Facebook Messenger button inviting people to send a message. That's what concerns me. Someone who just lost thousands of dollars could see this advertisement and believe they've finally found a solution. After all, it looks like a company offering specialized assistance. And because it appears as a paid Facebook advertisement, some people may assume the advertiser has been thoroughly vetted. The second screenshot Patrick sent us is even more troubling. It shows a Facebook page displaying the title "Director of Fraud Investigations" and the name Grace K. The cover image features the White House, the FBI's J. Edgar Hoover Building and cryptocurrency graphics. It also displays references to IC3 and the U.S. Department of Justice. The page description claims to help fraud victims navigate the IC3 reporting process. It even suggests that people who lost more than $4,000 may qualify for federal review. That claim appears on the page, but we found no support for such a dollar threshold in the FBI's published guidance. It's a convincing presentation for someone desperately searching for help. The American flags and official-looking graphics create the impression that a federal agency may be involved. But here's what you need to know. The FBI says IC3 has no official social media presence. It never investigates crimes or recovers stolen money through Facebook Messenger or Telegram. That means any Facebook page claiming to represent IC3 should immediately raise suspicion, regardless of how official it looks. Meta's subsequent removal of the flagged accounts and advertisements reinforces those concerns. After CyberGuy shared Patrick's screenshots with Meta, the company investigated and confirmed that it removed the flagged accounts and…

articles.title: 19 Agent Skills Test Your Web App With Playwright and Real Browsers
articles.content: Nineteen open-licensed agent skills let an AI agent test a web app the way a person would: write the test first, open a real browser, click through the flows and report what broke. They come from Vercel Labs' agent-browser , Tech Leads Club , Anthropic , Matt Pocock, Jesse Vincent and lackeyjb . All 19 are packaged as the QA & Testing plugin in Cuttlefish.MD , HackerNoon's license-checked skills marketplace. They follow the open Agent Skills standard , so they run in Claude Code, Codex CLI and 30+ other tools , and each is indexed in HackerNoon's SKILL.md Library . The 19 QA and testing skills Skill What it does Author agent-browser A browser automation CLI built for AI agents Vercel Labs agentcore Runs agent-browser on AWS Bedrock AgentCore cloud browsers Vercel Labs chrome-devtools Debugs, profiles and automates the browser through the Chrome DevTools MCP server Tech Leads Club core The core agent-browser usage guide Vercel Labs demo Records a demo video of a feature on a real desktop with a real cursor Tech Leads Club derive-client Records browser traffic to reverse-engineer a site's internal API and generate a client Vercel Labs dogfood Explores a web app systematically to find bugs and UX problems Vercel Labs electron Automates Electron desktop apps such as VS Code, Slack and Figma Vercel Labs playwright-skill Full browser automation with Playwright lackeyjb playwright-skill Tech Leads Club's packaging of Playwright browser automation Tech Leads Club protected-vercel-deployments Tests Vercel deployments behind SSO or Deployment Protection Vercel Labs slack Works in Slack workspaces through browser automation Vercel Labs spec-driven-eval Grades how completely an implementation meets its PRD, case by case Tech Leads Club tdd Builds features and fixes bugs test-first, red-green-refactor Matt Pocock test-driven-development Writes the failing test before any implementation code Jesse Vincent tlc-spec-driven Plans and builds features in four phases: specify, design, tasks, execute Tech Leads Club vercel-sandbox Runs agent-browser and Chrome inside Vercel Sandbox microVMs Vercel Labs webapp-testing Tests local web apps with Playwright Anthropic webmcp-gen Builds and validates experimental WebMCP tools for a page Vercel Labs Install all 19 in one command /plugin marketplace add hackernoon/cuttlefish-agent-skills /plugin install qa-testing@cuttlefish For Codex CLI, Cursor or another agent that supports the standard, clone the repo and copy plugins/qa-testing/skills/ into your agent's skills folder, such as .agents/skills/ . The agent-browser skills need Vercel's agent-browser CLI installed. Each skill keeps its license and an ATTRIBUTION.md naming its author and source commit. Browse the full library at hackernoon.com/skills , and star Cuttlefish.MD on GitHub .

articles.title: Apple’s M5 MacBook Air is down to its lowest price since July
articles.content: A top-down view of the 15-inch MacBook Air, which features Apple’s M5 processor. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge The latest 13-inch MacBook Air is currently available for $1,099.99, marking the second time we’ve seen this $200 discount following the company’s hefty price increases over the summer . Although the base model — which features Apple’s M5 processor, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage — often sold for around $950 to $1,000 shortly after it launched in May, savings have been rare since July, making the current deal worth flagging. Amazon , Best Buy , and B&H Photo are all honoring the price across all color options. If you’d prefer something with a larger screen, a six-speaker array instead of four, and slightly more power (with two additional GPU cores in the M5), Apple’s 15-inch MacBook Air is also on sale for $200 off. Amazon , Best Buy , and B&H Photo are each selling the 16GB RAM / 512GB SSD configuration in most colors for $1,299.99. Apple 13-inch MacBook Air (M5) Where to Buy: $1299 $1099 at Amazon $1299 $1099 at Best Buy $1299 $1099 at B&H Photo Although it’s pricier than the newer MacBook Neo, the Air offers better value in numerous ways. It’s an ideal choice if you want faster performance, as it offers double the RAM and a speedier CPU with more cores. You also get twice as much storage, better speakers, a backlit keyboard, and a larger, higher-resolution screen. Given said differences, it’s easy to see how the Air’s improvements might make it worth the extra cost for some people. If you’re still on the fence, though, I’d recommend reading my colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto’s reviews, both of which were published before the summer price increases. Read our full MacBook Neo and M5 MacBook Air reviews.

articles.title: Apple Taking New Approach to Developing iOS 28 and macOS 28
articles.content: Apple has made a change to its development process for iOS 28, macOS 28, and corresponding software updates, according to Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman. In his Power On newsletter today , he said Apple separates development of each year's new operating systems into three major stages. Typically, he said each stage consists of four weeks of coding followed by a four-week "convergence" period where new features are integrated into the operating systems. This time around, Apple has made a change. The first stage of development for iOS 28 and the other updates apparently consisted of six weeks of coding and two weeks of feature convergence. This change gives Apple's software engineers more time to come up with new features. "Instead of the normal split between two four-week efforts, Apple engineers were tasked with six weeks of coding, exploration and feature development, and then only two weeks of convergence," he said. "Employees say they like the change, indicating that it creates more time for coming up with ideas and exploring them before needing to lock things in." Gurman did not reveal any specific features planned for iOS 28. The update should be available in beta in June and released in September next year. articles.title: Python's CVEs Triple. Anthropic Funds a New Security Developer
articles.content: In the last year CVEs have increased 3x for Python and its package manager Pip, according to Python's security developer in residence Seth Larson. "And the amount of malware published and removed from the Python Package Index (PyPI) is up 60%." Securing Python's ecosystem is getting more complex, he writes, especially given "the evolving role of AI in both security risks and security response." Their response includes bringing on a new Security Developer "to address the increasingly demanding scale of security response for the Python ecosystem." Providing prompt security response services and innovating to prevent future threats... is more difficult now than ever before... [Security developer Brett Smith] will help us keep pace with critical ongoing work such as vulnerability remediation, providing vulnerability data as a CVE Numbering Authority, and removing malware from PyPI. He'll also give the team bandwidth for new projects such as scaling PyPI's autonomous quarantine program to reduce manual effort on malware remediation and streamlining processes for the PSRT to handle the new vulnerability report volume. The role was made possible by an "ecosystem security" grant from Anthropic. And having the new security developer "will both build capacity for security work the PSF already does and enable new, proactive work," concludes Python's security developer in residence. (He discussed Python's security challenges in a June presentation with Python security engineer Mike Fiedler> .) In June, Curl's Daniel Strenberg reported Curl's CVEs have also tripled. articles.title: Perplexity’s AI agents keep working after you close the tab
articles.content: Perplexity’s new Teammates can coordinate multiple agents, remember where previous sessions left off, and keep working without another prompt. The challenge is keeping everything in sync, especially when agents are working at the same time, sharing project state, and operating with different permissions. Announced Wednesday , Teammates builds on infrastructure Perplexity has spent much of the year developing. The launch puts that earlier work to use in workflows where agents can delegate tasks and continue operating across sessions. The challenge of keeping agents stateful When Nate Kupp , Perplexity’s vice president of infrastructure, took The New Stack inside the company’s agent sandboxes , he described the difficulty of maintaining reliable systems at that scale. “Stateful systems are incredibly hard to build,” Kupp said, pointing to the durability and uptime requirements of operating millions of sandboxes. “Stateful systems are incredibly hard to build” Teammates relies on Perplexity Computer’s existing infrastructure, which separates persistent project state from individual execution environments. That allows agents to continue working on the same project without depending on a single uninterrupted session. Shared state lives in Git In a technical breakdown of its shared workspaces , the company described how it uses Git-backed repositories to keep project state intact across sessions. Each Computer project has its own repository, while agents work in separate sandboxes and submit their changes back to the shared project. That gets more complicated when agents are working on the same code at once since if one agent commits its changes first, another may have to reapply its work against the latest version. Perplexity says fewer than 2% of submissions are rejected because they’re based on outdated repository state. Median submission latency is under 1.7 seconds, while p99 stays below eight seconds. Median submission latency is under 1.7 seconds, while p99 stays below eight seconds. Memory is handled separately through Perplexity’s Brain system, which keeps what agents have learned in dedicated repositories. That lets background agents update shared knowledge without interfering with changes to the project’s files. Pausing and forking agents Perplexity built SPACE around Firecracker microVMs and Btrfs snapshots, making it possible to pause, resume, or fork agent sessions without losing their saved state. With Teammates, developers can connect tools like Slack and GitHub and set up triggers that tell agents when to act. Perplexity hasn’t said much about what happens when that work gets stuck, particularly when one agent is waiting on another or acting on information that’s already out of date. The open permission questions Each teammate runs in its own isolated environment and browser session, with access managed through Computer’s existing permissions and credentials handled securely through encryption. Users can also monitor progress and take control when needed. It’s unclear how it prevents agents from accessing resources beyond their permissions when tasks are handed off. For enterprises, that uncertainty could influence how much autonomy they’re willing to give agents without requiring human approval. Teammates is initially available on the web for Perplexity Max subscribers, with iOS support planned. articles.title: Diamond Foundry creates world's first 200mm single-crystal diamond wafer
articles.content: Diamonds have exceptional cooling capabilities due to their excellent thermal conductivity, with the material estimated to be at least five times more conductive than copper . Because of this, Diamond Foundry, a firm focusing on lab-grown diamonds, announced the world’s first 200mm single-crystal diamond (SCD) wafer. The 200mm SCD is about the same wafer size that semiconductor fabs use for older processes, with the company boasting on its website that “Single-crystal diamond has entered the wafer-scale era.” This is part of the effort to manufacture SCD at scale so that it can be used for semiconductor cooling, especially now that increasing power of AI chips has also led to enormous thermal problems. What makes Diamond Foundry’s 200mm SCD wafer different from other lab-grown diamonds is that it’s created as a high-quality single-crystal piece instead of a polycrystalline gem. Although the former is difficult to manufacture, it is what allows diamond to become an extreme efficient thermal conductor while simultaneously retaining its electrical insulating properties — this efficiency should help cut down on hotspots, making SCDs an excellent solution for AI chip cooling. The company also showed in a graph that it is now thought possible to create a D300 SCD wafer before 2030, matching the size of the wafers used in leading node processes. However, it should be noted that the sample shown by the company remains unpolished, meaning it still needs to go through some processes to make it suitable for chipmakers. (Image credit: Diamond Foundry ) Although the company was founded in 2012, it also acknowledged the work of scientists who have been chipping away at the scale problem of SCDs since the early 2000s. “This is one of those milestones that once seemed almost impossible. Hundreds of DF engineers, scientists, and technicians contributed to us getting here. It is the accumulated result of countless experiments, failures, inventions, rebuilt machines, and insights over more than a decade,” Diamond Foundry CEO Martin Roscheisen said. “Stefan and Martin pursued this goal for 25 years. There are very few examples in technology of someone sticking to a really hard scientific challenge with that level of perseverance. They kept going when the prevailing view was that single‑crystal diamond simply could not be made at this scale. Today, the perseverance shows as the first-ever D200mm single‑crystal diamond. And best of all, it makes D300mm predictable as well.” Diamond Foundry Diamond Foundry Diamond Foundry isn’t the only company that has identified the potential of lab-grown diamonds for semiconductor cooling. Akash Systems secured $18.2 million in CHIPS Act funding in 2024 to produce Gallium Nitride fused with synthetic diamond , which it claims will reduce temperatures by 20 degrees C. The De Beers Group, which is known for its diamond mines in Africa, is also building a copper-plated diamond composite material aimed at improving cooling efficiency for AI, high-performance computing, and GaN RF devices. Even Frore Systems, which is known for its solid-state cooler , is diving into diamond-infused watercooling cold plates for Nvidia’s next-generation AI GPUs.

articles.title: Logitech G502 X Lightspeed Review: No lights, same price
articles.content: Logitech's G502 X Lightspeed has been around for awhile — the mouse was introduced in 2022 alongside the fancier Logitech G502 X Plus (and the wired G502 X), but since it’s receiving a firmware update that upgrades its Hero 25K sensor to a Hero 44K sensor, this seemed like a good time to take a look at it. The G502X Lightspeed is available in black and white colorways and currently retails for $159.99, which is the same price as the G502 X Plus — however, it can (and should) normally be found for less than this. Design and Comfort of the G502 X Lightspeed The Logitech G502 X Lightspeed is a right-handed gaming mouse with an ergonomically contoured shape. It's the same size and shape as the G502 X Plus, with large primary mouse buttons, textured rubber side panels for grip, and a smooth matte chassis with glossy accents. It comes in black and white colorways (our review unit was black) and has no lighting aside from a small indicator light at the front of the mouse to indicate connection and battery life. Like the G502 X Plus, the G502 X Lightspeed is definitely on the larger side. It measures 5.17 inches (131.4mm) long by 3.12 inches (79.2mm) wide, and is 1.62 inches (41.1mm) high at its tallest point. It's larger than the Razer Basilisk V3 Pro and V4 Pro (5.11 x 2.96 x 1.67 inches / 130 x 75.4 x 42.5mm) — not by a lot, but it definitely feels like a much larger mouse. It weighs about 3.6 ounces (102g), which makes it lighter than the Basilisk V3 Pro, but slightly heavier than the Basilisk V4 Pro. Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware The G502 X Lightspeed has 11 programmable buttons, and 13 programmable controls if you include scroll up/down. There are the left and right primary mouse buttons, as well as two side buttons along the left edge of the left mouse button. On the left side of the mouse there are the two standard thumb buttons, plus a "sniper" button that's magnetically attached and can be flipped so that it's not in your way. The sniper button can also be "deleted," and Logitech includes a delete cover in the box that makes the button unpressable (and also has the same soft, rubbery texture as the rest of the thumb rest). articles.title: Japanese arcades suffer week-long blackout following Sega server hack
articles.content: The sensory overload typically experienced when visiting video game arcades in Japan was eerily absent from some venues this week, reports ITMedia News [machine translation]. It says that a Sega system outage meant there was “no end in sight” for the rows of silent black screens. However, a recent tweet from arcade network operator ALL.net indicates that both Sega and Bandai Namco machines are affected. Moreover, arcade lovers will be pleased to hear that affected arcades will “gradually resume operation on a trial basis starting today.” a friend sent me some pics of their local arcade and LMAO the sega outage is nuts https://t.co/3vSYjCYAIZ November 3, 2026 ALL.Net, a contraction of Amusement Linkage Live Network, was launched by Sega in 2004 to allow arcade games to look up to the net for auto updates, data logging, implement online play, and power national leaderboards. Sega titles like Initial D The Arcade, Maimai, and CHUNITHM , rely on this network, as do Bandai Namco games like A iko no Tatsujin, Mario Kart Arcade GP DX, and Gundam Extreme Vs . Some services are gradually resuming operation today. (Image credit: ALL.Net, Sega Fave ) In its official apology blog post, dated November 2, ALL.Net / Sega Fave said that it suspended services a day prior after it became aware of its servers being affected by “unauthorized access by a third party.” It reassured customers that their personal info and billing data were not on the compromised server. However, it asked for more time to investigate, run safety checks, and so on, before restoring service. This morning ALL.Net told customers that Bandia Namco titles “will gradually resume operation on a trial basis starting today (online play and card use enabled).” Sega products remain under maintenance, and online services are unavailable. There is currently no estimate for issue resolution, but a news bulletin is promised for November 10 (Tuesday). Classic offline arcade machines weren’t affected by this outage, of course. Moreover, rival arcade gaming legends like Taito and Konami run their own, separate, arcade networks and authentication systems.

articles.title: The end of an era as Linux 7.5 purges the last 30-year-old Intel MMX optimizations from Pentium age
articles.content: Linux developers are preparing to make Intel’s ancient MultiMedia eXtensions an irrelevance. Intel introduced MMX in the Pentium era, but a patch expected to merge into mainline Linux 7.5 will remove the last remaining optimized software from the open-source OS. Expected to be released in 2027, the new kernel will wipe MMX-optimized code from its software RAID XOR code, explains Phoronix . Admittedly, there wasn’t much left in Linux in terms of MMX optimizations. But few folks will be running the most modern kernels on Pentium MMX and Pentium II chips in 2026. And most other MMX-optimized code disappeared from the OS half a decade ago, when some MMX-optimized memory management code was removed. Note that, if you are a determined late-90s Pentium devotee, you can still use software RAID, but it will lack the MMX fast path. This is a classic case of Linux code housekeeping. With this change, the kernel will lose over 800 lines of code and replace them with just 12. Remembering MMX Intel first introduced MMX Pentium chips in January 1997. Though I vaguely remember these processors being marketed as being enhanced by ‘MultiMedia eXtensions,’ Wikipedia insists that “MMX is officially a meaningless initialism[6] trademarked by Intel.” In a subsequent trademark battle with longtime foe AMD, a document produced in court indicated that MMX stood for ‘Matrix Math Extensions.’ AMD relied on this to sidestep the trademark, as an initialism cannot be trademarked, according to the encyclopedic source. Eventually, all rival x86 processors managed to integrate MMX instructions – so as not to be pushed into the shade during the multimedia boom. A surprisingly large number of non-Intel chips ended up offering MMX, too. Along with Pentium MMX chips, AMD, Centaur, Cyrix , Rise, and Transmeta eventually offered MMX CPUs. After MMX's marketing success, AMD pioneered 3DNow! instructions , and about a year later, Intel fired back with SSE and SSE2.

articles.title: Ukraine builds combat robots to hunt Russian troops in underground gas pipelines
articles.content: Ukraine is developing a new class of combat robots designed to operate inside underground gas pipelines, where Russian troops have repeatedly attempted to bypass frontline defenses, United24Media reports. The project, disclosed by Ukraine's 2 nd National Guard Corps, Khartiia, involves modifying unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) to perform reconnaissance and combat missions in spaces too narrow for conventional military machinery. Notably, the work is being carried out by specialists from the corps’ Lava Unmanned Systems Regiment, following Operation Veles — an underground assault that saw Ukrainian soldiers advance more than 15 kilometers through pipeline infrastructure near Kupiansk. Khartiia says the operation killed more than 100 enemy soldiers and resulted in over 30 captured, although those battlefield figures have not been independently verified. The commander of Lavas ground robotic system battalion, identified by the callsign ‘Matematyk’, said the project addresses a category of warfare that requires a different approach from conventional battlefield robotics. “There is a very long list of tasks that need to be accomplished to fight underground and counter the enemy underground. This is a new class of technologies and challenges that we will have to confront,” he said. The machines are being adapted from existing groundrobots ,rather than developed as conventional surface vehicles. They must be compact enough to navigate narrow pipelines while retaining the ability to carry out military assignments . Most commercially available underground machinery, meanwhile, is designed for construction, drilling, and tunneling — not combat. As of now, Khartiia is already developing several robotic systems to address those limitations, with the broader objective of sending machines into dangerous underground environments where soldiers would otherwise have to conduct reconnaissance, confront enemy positions, clear positions, or clear out themselves. “War is already underground, and it will expand. The question is how we adapt to this war,” Matematyk said. The project follows unusual battlefield developments near Kupiansk, where Ukrainian forces used the same underground infrastructure that Russian troops have previously exploited to infiltrate behind Ukrainian defensive positions. During Operation Vels, Ukrainian soldiers moved through a gas pipeline measuring approximately 1.2 meters in diameter, according to a report by Ikrainska Pravda. The confined passage made movement and close-range firefights particularly,with Ukrainian troops having little-to-no room to maneuver. Russia had previously used the pipeline network beneath the Oskil River to move soldiers toward Ukrainian-held territory. The Ukrainian battlefield monitoring group ‘Deepstate' reported an earlier Russian infiltration attempt in September 2025. Last month, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukrainian forces had eliminated more than 100 Russian troops and captured over 30 during the operation. The experience also exposed the limitation of sending soldiers into such environments. Underground operations restrict visibility,complicate communications , and leave little room for maneuvering equipment. That said, Ukraine has increased its reliance on unmanned military systems as battlefield terrain proves complicated to navigate. In July 2024, we reported on Ukrainian forces deploying AI-controlled drones capable of independently identifying and attaching targets. The country has also been experimenting with unmanned systems that operate beyond conventional aerial platforms. In August, the US Army tested an autonomous Ford F-250 breaching vehicle , which builds on the Lancer unmanned ground vehicle program and uses a counter-drone turret to protect military operations from aerial attacks. However, autonomous ground systems still face considerable technical challenges. Russia's Shturm uncrewed assault tanks , for instance , repeatedly lost their command connection…

articles.title: How Apple's Personal Knowledge Graph learns about your life on Mac
articles.content: A breakdown of Apple's Personal Knowledge Graph shows what your Mac and Apple Intelligence know about you and your life. An example of contextual Siri on Mac The upgrade to Siri AI added the understanding of personal context to Apple Intelligence . By pulling information from messages, emails, and photos, Siri can come up with answers to queries with contextual elements, such as knowing the name of your mother from a travel itinerary. However, Apple has been compiling data on its users for a lot longer, with macOS 13 doing so since 2022. In a breakdown by security researchers at Eighth Rank, the generation of a Personal Knowledge Graph in macOS is detailed, including the kinds of data it compiles and retains on your Mac. articles.title: Nvidia released its 8800 GTX GPU 20 years ago today, celebrates with Steam game homage
articles.content: On this day in 2006, Nvidia released the legendary GeForce 8800 GTX and 8800 GTS graphics cards . Nvidia has decided to honor the flagship of the pair with its GeForce 8800 GTX - 20 Years of a Legend interactive demo, now free on Steam . However, the recommended specs to ‘play’ with this semi-interactive path-traced unboxing experience include a wallet-worrying RTX 5080 . Or you could just watch the video, embedded below for your convenience. The downloadable demo, which also requires 32GB of RAM and 30GB of free storage, was created by Dylan Browne, a senior special effects artist who frequently works with Unreal Engine , as in this case. This experience is said to deliver era-appropriate graphics, but requires the most advanced graphics tech available two decades after the 8800 GTX first hit the scene to work its graphical magic. To run GeForce 8800 GTX - 20 Years of a Legend on a 2026 PC, you will need at least an RTX 4070 for acceptable performance, according to the Steam page. This software is stuffed with the latest graphics tech embraced by the green team. “DLSS 4.5 with Dynamic Multi Frame Generation, Ray Reconstruction, path tracing, and Mega Geometry” are all present, says Nvidia. Nvidia, Steam, Dylan Browne Nvidia, Steam, Dylan Browne Nvidia, Steam, Dylan Browne There’s a bit more to the interactive demo than looking around and poking a box with your mouse and then prodding it to fit the shiny new GPU into your “era-accurate PC tower.” An extra layer of fun is promised by the provision of hidden Easter eggs in this experience. However, the demo appears to show Windows Vista on the PC in the gaming den, which launched at retail a few months after the 8800 GTX. Admittedly, this legendary GeForce card and Windows Vista OS would roam the Earth at the same time, with many folks buying the GeForce 8800 GTX and 8800 GTS to shove into their Vista PCs from 2007 onwards. Crysis launched on PCs in late 2007, a year after the G80 architecture cards debuted. Nvidia launched the GeForce 8800 GTX (128 shader units) and 8800 GTS (96 shader units) at $599 and $449, respectively. These legendary Nvidia GPUs spearheaded the DirectX 10 era, accelerating existing PC titles and delivering next-gen visuals with new DX10 software. You can read more in our reviews from the time, like the 12-page review of the GeForce 8800 GTX and GTS from the launch week. Briefly, our reviewer thought these cards were “amazing” for their current performance and DX10 promise . They were also excited about the G80 architecture for bringing CUDA to consumers and the promise of making the GPU “something much more than a frame rendering device.” Some Luddite gamers may wish that had never happened. Future Future Nvidia driver support for the GeForce 8800 GTX and GTS would run out of road about a decade later. By that time, DirectX 11 hardware and games were mainstream, leaving older graphics hardware designs obsolete when it came to playing the latest AAA PC titles.
